construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor precision when sliding many beads (tap-to-fill and snap-to-count reduce it); rewarding raw speed on compares (credit only accuracy-held speed via M-SPEEDACC, never the fastest tap); density/size confounds in nonsymbolic compares (control bead spacing and include size-number-incongruent rows); reading removed via spoken and pictured prompts; keep EQUAL reachable to avoid position bias.

name: Hanging Mobile Balancer
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: choose the weight(s) that keep a balance scale in equilibrium (Figure Weights)
number_sentence_building: enter values to balance both sides of an equation
mathematical-equivalence items (meaning of the equal sign, e.g. 3+4=_+5)
arithmetic_reasoning
proportional_reasoning: ratio/rate reasoning via lever distance (torque)
one_liner: The child hangs shapes on the hooks of a tilting mobile so every arm hangs perfectly level, discovering the weight or position that makes both sides equal.
interaction: A mobile hangs from a pivot: a horizontal bar with hooks at marked distances on each side (older levels add a second sub-bar). Each shape carries a hidden weight shown as pips. The child drags shapes onto hooks (or into an empty target hook) and the bar tilts in real time toward the heavier turning-effect side; when both sides match, the bar snaps level and glows. Tasks: make it hang level, or choose which single weight fills the empty hook to balance. Submission = Lock when level. A missing-addend / non-canonical variant pre-loads unequal sides so only a relational solution levels it, and for older bands hook distance matters so a light shape far out can balance a heavy shape near in.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the left hook holds 3 pips and the right holds 1 so the bar tips left; the hand drags a 2-pip shape onto the right and the bar swings level with a settle and chime, then repeats once. One unscored warm-up hangs one apple opposite one apple to level a simple bar. The tilt makes level-means-equal obvious with no words.

learning_science.principle: Rule-based development of balance-scale reasoning (weight then distance)
learning_science.why: Children progress through identifiable rules on balance tasks - weight-only, then integrating distance - so a mobile is a validated probe that scales from concrete equality to multiplicative torque reasoning within one shell.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer weight-only leveling for young bands and distance-matters (torque) items for older bands, and infer the child's rule level from which items they can balance.
learning_science.source: Siegler & Chen (1998), 'Developmental differences in rule learning: A microgenetic analysis', Cognitive Psychology 36(3):273-310.

learning_science.principle: Relational meaning of the equal sign
learning_science.why: A relational view of equality (both sides name the same amount) rather than an operational one uniquely predicts later algebra success, and leveling a pre-loaded unequal mobile requires that relational view.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-canonical pre-loaded sides and classify the child's first hang as relational (targets the needed remainder) or operational (dumps a running total).
learning_science.source: Kieran (1981), 'Concepts associated with the equality symbol', Educational Studies in Mathematics 12(3):317-326.

tail_precision_rationale: The equivalence signature (M-EQREL) from the first hang flags relational versus operational thinking - a research-backed early separator of algebra-ready reasoning invisible to a right/wrong score - while on distance items the proportional-strategy signature (M-PROPSTRAT) distinguishes children who trade weight against distance multiplicatively from those who only add weight; efficiency-vs-optimal and revisions separate direct computers from tilt-guided trial and error.
age_rationale: As a concrete make-it-hang-straight matching task the mobile is accessible at K-1 (equal counts on symmetric hooks); genuine equivalence reasoning (missing-addend, non-canonical sides) emerges at 2-3 and up, and distance/torque proportional balancing is reserved for 6-8. The drag-to-hook interaction is constant, and the K-8 tag reflects one shell spanning concrete equality through pre-algebraic torque via adaptive difficulty.

adaptive.content_range: concrete symmetric leveling with equal counts (K-1) through non-canonical missing-addend equivalence (2-3/4-5) and multiplicative distance/torque balancing that encodes proportional relationships without notation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of hooks and shapes, canonical vs non-canonical pre-load, weight-only vs distance-matters, integer vs fractional weights, and number of empty target hooks
adaptive.notes: Hook loads and distances are generated from equivalence and torque templates; the operational-trap load is computed for M-EQREL and the optimal hang count for M-EFF.

engagement_hook: A dangling mobile that sways and teeters like a real hanging sculpture and snaps satisfyingly level when balanced turns equivalence and lever reasoning into a mobile-building game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag motor load (snap-to-hook, large shapes); pure tilt-guided trial and error (captured via M-EFF and the first-hang M-EQREL rather than penalized, with some commit-blind items in the bank); reading removed via pips and icons; tilt state shown by angle and a level-line, not color alone; distance items use clearly marked hook positions so the lever arm is perceivable.

name: Number Tug-of-War
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: keep the rope centered by making both teams' totals equal
quantitative_comparison: greater / less / equal
compare two magnitudes and judge greater / less / equal
number_sentence_building: enter values to make both sides equal
number_sense_magnitude
one_liner: Two teams of numbered characters pull a rope; the child taps the stronger side, or adds characters so the totals match and the flag stays centered.
interaction: A rope with a center flag stretches between two teams. Each character shows a number (its pull) and the total pull on each side moves the flag proportionally, so the bigger total drags the flag toward it. Two modes: (a) compare - the teams flash and the child taps the side that will win, or a center TIE button when equal; (b) balance - the child drags numbered characters onto a team (or into an empty slot) until both totals match and the flag locks at center. Submission = single tap (compare) or Lock at center (balance).
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the left team totals 5 and the right totals 3 so the flag slides left and the left team cheers; the hand then drags a 2 onto the right, the totals read 5 and 5, and the flag snaps to center with a chime. One unscored warm-up shows 2 versus 1 and the hand taps the stronger side. The flag's motion makes more-pull-wins and equal-pull-ties obvious wordlessly.

learning_science.why: Judging which of two quantities is greater draws on an analogue magnitude representation whose precision indexes numerical ability and is measurable before formal arithmetic, letting young children demonstrate quantitative reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale the difference between the two team totals adaptively (a distance/ratio staircase) and credit accuracy-held speed on the tap-the-winner mode.
learning_science.source: Dehaene, Dupoux & Mehler (1990), 'Is numerical comparison digital? Analogical and symbolic effects in two-digit number comparison', Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance 16(3):626-641.

learning_science.principle: Central conceptual structure for number (compare and equalize)
learning_science.why: A mental-number-line central conceptual structure lets children coordinate comparison and equalization of quantities, the reasoning behind making two sides fair, and its development marks quantitative competence in the early grades.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an equalize (make-it-fair) mode requiring the child to add exactly the difference to the smaller side, and score whether the first move targets that difference.
learning_science.source: Case & Okamoto (1996), 'The role of central conceptual structures in the development of children's thought', Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development 61(1-2).

tail_precision_rationale: On the speeded compare mode the joint speed-accuracy operating point and false-alarm rate separate careful-fast (able) responders from impulsive fast-wrong ones so raw speed is never rewarded; on the balance mode revisions and whether the first move equals the exact difference reveal direct computation versus trial and error, adding process variance beyond correctness at the cut.
age_rationale: Tapping the stronger team is a K-1-level judgement and adding one character to make a tie is within K-1 counting; totals, team sizes, number formats, and the closeness of the two totals escalate for older bands, and 6-8 can face multi-member sums and fractions. The tap/drag interaction is constant, reading is removed, and K-8 marks one shell spanning the whole range via adaptive closeness.

adaptive.content_range: compare and equalize within 10 with obvious differences (K-1) through multi-member two-digit or fractional totals with near-equal sides (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: total magnitude, closeness of the two totals (distance/ratio), number of members per team, integer vs fractional pulls, compare vs equalize mode, and flashed-then-masked vs static
adaptive.notes: Teams are generated from target totals with a computed difference; the closeness staircase feeds M-SPEEDACC and the equalize target feeds first-move scoring.

engagement_hook: A lively rope that lurches toward the stronger team and a flag that snaps to center on a perfect tie make comparison and equalizing feel like refereeing a playground contest.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Speed pressure inducing impulsive taps (credit only accuracy-held speed and log M-FALSEALARM; anticipatory taps under a floor are discounted); motor load (large team drop zones, single-tap compare); reading removed via numerals and icons; flag position readable by displacement and a center line, not color alone; keep TIE equally reachable to avoid position bias.

name: Number Grid Lock
topics_techniques_covered: numeric_matrix: find the missing number that satisfies a matrix of relations
number_analogies: infer the quantitative relation in a 2x2 and complete it
number_series
Number Series: determine the missing number in a sequence
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
one_liner: The child cracks a numeric safe by dialing the missing number(s) so every row and column of the grid satisfies its hidden relation.
interaction: A safe's dial-grid shows numbers with one (or more) blank cell. Each row and each column follows a relation (a constant step, a sum, or a multiply). The child selects a blank and dials its value with plus/minus wheels or taps a candidate; a row or column clicks and lights when its relation is satisfied, and the lock opens when all lines hold. A K-1 entry uses a single row (a counting/skip series); 2x2 grids introduce a cross relation (analogy); 3x3 grids require row and column relations at once. Submission = Open (commit) once the cells are set.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): a 2x2 shows 2,4 over 3,? with a glowing x2 arrow across the top row; the hand dials the bottom-right to 6 so the column and row both click and the lock pops open with a chime. One unscored warm-up is a single row 1,2,3,? dialed to 4. The clicking lines teach make-every-line's-pattern-true without words.

learning_science.principle: Component processes of analogical and relational inference
learning_science.why: Solving a numeric analogy or matrix requires encoding elements, inferring the relation, and mapping and applying it - separable reasoning components whose demand marks higher quantitative reasoning distinct from calculation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Design distractors so each foil satisfies some but not all relations, so the chosen value reveals which relational components the child applied, and tag errors to the missed relation.
learning_science.source: Sternberg (1977), 'Component processes in analogical reasoning', Psychological Review 84(4):353-378.

learning_science.principle: Rule abstraction and goal management in matrices
learning_science.why: Matrix-reasoning ability is driven by the number of relational rules a solver can induce and manage toward the goal cell simultaneously, which is a strong marker of fluid and quantitative reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale the number of co-acting row/column rules and record the maximum simultaneously satisfied rules on correct high-complexity locks (rule dimensionality).
learning_science.source: Carpenter, Just & Shell (1990), 'What one intelligence test measures: A theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test', Psychological Review 97(3):404-431.

tail_precision_rationale: Rule dimensionality solved (M-RULEID) exposes how many co-acting row/column relations a child binds at once - separating two correct children at 1 versus 3 simultaneous rules where a single difficulty index blurs them - while first-action latency indexes reflective encoding, hint-free solving is stronger evidence, and M-DIFFREACH over grid size and rule count pinpoints the relational ceiling that most sharply separates the upper tail.
age_rationale: The lock shell degrades gracefully to a single-row counting/skip series that K-1 can crack, becomes a 2x2 cross-relation (analogy) at 2-3, a 3x3 single-rule matrix at 4-5, and a 3x3 with two co-acting row/column rules and larger or fractional numbers at 6-8; dialing or tapping a cell is low motor and notation-free, and K-8 marks the one shell spanning counting series to relational matrices via adaptive complexity.

adaptive.content_range: single-row counting/skip series (K-1) through 3x3 two-rule numeric matrices with larger or fractional entries (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size (1 row to 3x3), number of co-acting rules, relation type (additive/multiplicative/mixed), number of blanks, number magnitude/format, and candidate-tap vs free-dial entry
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated by sampling row/column relations then blanking cells; foils are keyed to individual missed relations for M-RULEID and error typing, and grid size and rule count set M-DIFFREACH.

engagement_hook: Each satisfied row or column clicks like a safe tumbler and the lock springs open when every line is true, turning numeric-matrix and series reasoning into cracking a vault.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Dial/keypad motor and numeral load (offer candidate-tap for young bands); trial-and-error dialing using the click cues (captured via M-RTFIRST, M-HINT and commit-blind locks in the bank); no reading required (numerals and iconic relation arrows); the satisfied-line cue is shown by a lit outline and a click, not color alone; cap magnitudes so the relation, not computation, is the bottleneck.

name: Quantitative Reasoning Quest
topics_techniques_covered: quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
number_series
numeric_matrix
balance_equivalence
quantitative_comparison
word_problem_reasoning
proportional_reasoning
one_liner: The child travels a quest map where each gate is a short number challenge in a different format - compare, series, matrix, balance, ratio, or a pictured story - routed to stay at the edge of what they can do.
interaction: An avatar advances along a path of gates. Each gate poses one bite-size item drawn from a rotating set of formats: tap-the-greater (comparison), tap the next term (series), dial the missing cell (matrix), pick the weight that balances (equivalence), pick the equal ratio (proportion), or solve a pictured/audio one-step story (word problem). The child answers with a single tap or a dial; a correct answer advances the avatar and steps difficulty up, a miss steps difficulty down (adaptive routing). Some gates are matched clones of an earlier format to check consistency. Submission = per-gate tap/confirm; the run ends after a fixed number of gates or at a stable ceiling.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the avatar reaches a compare gate and the hand taps the bigger of two groups to open it and step forward, then a series gate opens by tapping the next number; each format shows its own tiny ghost-hand the first time it appears. One unscored warm-up gate (compare 2 vs 5) starts the run. Because every gate reuses the wordless conventions of the single-format types, each new format self-teaches in one animated beat.

learning_science.why: Routing each item to the child's current ability holds measurement near the person's edge, which minimizes the standard error exactly at the high cut where fixed forms are least informative.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Step difficulty up on success and down on failure across a wide above-level bank so the run converges on the child's ceiling with few items.
learning_science.source: Weiss (1982), 'Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing', Applied Psychological Measurement 6(4):473-492.

learning_science.why: Interleaving different problem formats forces the solver to identify which kind of reasoning each item needs, discriminating flexible quantitative reasoners from those who only pattern-match a single practiced format.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Randomly interleave formats rather than blocking them, and log per-format accuracy to profile breadth versus a narrow spike.
learning_science.source: Rohrer & Taylor (2007), 'The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning', Instructional Science 35(6):481-498.

tail_precision_rationale: Adaptive routing drives M-DIFFREACH (the ceiling reached across formats) as the sharpest single tail statistic, while cross-format consistency (M-CONSIST) on interleaved matched clones lowers the conditional standard error near the cut and flags spiky single-format performers; the progress trajectory (M-PROG) and end-of-run drift (M-DRIFT) turn one longer session into a curve and gate the decision on sustained engagement rather than a fatigued tail.
age_rationale: The quest starts every child at easy, K-1-appropriate gates (compare, count-on) and routes upward, so the same shell serves all bands; the hardest gates (multi-rule matrices, proportional and multi-step story gates) only appear for children who climb to them, so no band faces items beyond its reach. The single-tap/dial answers are low motor and reading is removed by spoken plus pictured gates, and K-8 marks the deliberately full-range adaptive span.

adaptive.content_range: count/compare gates (K-1) through multi-rule matrix, proportional, and multi-step story gates (6-8), blended and adaptively routed
adaptive.difficulty_levers: the per-format difficulty levers of each embedded format, plus routing step size, format mix, and clone-consistency rate
adaptive.notes: Gates are generated by the same parametric families as the single-format types; interleaving and the up/down routing are configuration, and matched clones across the run feed M-CONSIST.

engagement_hook: A quest where every gate is a fresh little puzzle and the avatar keeps climbing toward tougher challenges makes a full quantitative-reasoning battery feel like leveling up through a game world.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Format novelty and game-familiarity variance (each format keeps its wordless ghost-hand and an unscored first appearance); reading removed via spoken plus pictured gates; motor kept to a single tap or dial; adaptive routing must not trap a child in one format (enforce a minimum format spread); engagement and fatigue are monitored via M-DRIFT so late low-effort gates are down-weighted rather than scored as ability.

name: Turn-to-Match
topics_techniques_covered: mental_rotation
one_liner: The child drags a shape around to spin it until it lines up with a rotated target outline, then locks it in.
interaction: Drag anywhere on the movable piece to rotate it about its center; it snaps to the nearest allowed angle (90 degrees for K-1, 45/30 degrees for older). When the piece overlaps the dashed ghost target within tolerance it snaps green and the LOCK button enables; tapping LOCK submits. A 3D multiple-choice shell instead asks the child to tap the one candidate that is a pure rotation (not a mirror image) of the target.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand grabs the piece, sweeps it around until it aligns with the dashed target, and it clicks green with a chime; then one unscored warm-up lets the child rotate-and-lock before any scoring.

learning_science.principle: Mental rotation is an analog, time-scaled internal transformation (chronometric)
learning_science.why: Response time rises roughly linearly with angular disparity, so rotation is a measurable process rather than a guess, and its rate indexes ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Vary target angular disparity across trials (45-180 degrees) and record RT against angle to estimate each child's rotation rate.
learning_science.source: Shepard & Metzler (1971), Science 171:701-703, 'Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects'.

learning_science.principle: Spatial-skill gaps shrink with familiar, manipulable formats and practice (malleability)
learning_science.why: Mental-rotation performance depends heavily on strategy and comfort, which self-teaching demos and direct manipulation equalize across groups.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a wordless ghost-hand plus free drag-to-rotate with snap so the score reflects rotation, not instructions or pointer precision.
learning_science.source: Uttal, Meadow, Tipton, Hand, Alden, Warren & Newcombe (2013), Psychological Bulletin 139(2):352-402, 'The malleability of spatial skills: a meta-analysis of training studies'.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Mental-rotation RT slope
new_measurements_proposed.what: Slope of correct-trial response time regressed on target angular disparity.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The classic Shepard-Metzler chronometric signature; a shallow slope held at high accuracy is a rate-of-mental-transformation measure that is hard to coach and finely separates the spatial tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Present matched trials at several angular disparities and regress correct-trial RT on angle per child.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=12 trials spanning >=3 disparities for a stable slope estimate.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Mirror false-alarm rate
new_measurements_proposed.what: Rate of selecting an enantiomorph (mirror-image) foil instead of a true rotation.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Distinguishes genuine 3D mental rotation from partial feature-matching; low mirror false alarms at high disparity is a clean tail separator.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Include exact mirror foils and log the chirality of the chosen distractor.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=8 trials that contain a mirror foil.

tail_precision_rationale: Angular-disparity RT slope (M-ROTSLOPE) and mirror false-alarm rate (M-MIRRORFA) separate children who truly rotate objects from those who feature-match; at the gifted cut a shallow RT-vs-angle slope held at high accuracy with near-zero mirror errors on 150-180 degree items (M-DIFFREACH) is a hard-to-coach signature that CogAT's spatial-light battery misses.
age_rationale: K-1 uses 2D single shapes, 90-degree snap, and large hit targets so limited fine-motor control never blocks a correct rotation judgment; 2-3 adds 45-degree snaps and mirror foils; 4-5 introduces 3D block figures at moderate disparity; 6-8 uses Shepard-Metzler 3D figures up to 180 degrees with mirror distractors. Precise free-hand angle setting is hard for young children, so snapping preserves the construct (rotation) while removing motor noise.

adaptive.content_range: 2D letter/shape rotation (K-1) to 3D multi-limb Shepard-Metzler figures at 180 degrees with mirror foils (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: angular disparity; 2D vs 3D; number of object limbs/segments; snap granularity; presence and similarity of mirror foil; time pressure
adaptive.notes: Figures and target angles are procedurally generated from a parametric shape plus a rotation matrix, and mirror foils are exact reflections, so unlimited matched clones exist at any fixed difficulty.

engagement_hook: Feels like turning a key or spinning a dial until it clicks; the satisfying green snap plus chime rewards precise alignment and invites 'just one more'.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor control (mitigated by snap and large targets); device (touch vs mouse rotation feel, normalize RT within device); familiarity with rotation games (mitigated by ghost-hand and warm-up); visual crowding for 3D figures (control limb count).

name: Shape-Fill Form Board
topics_techniques_covered: form_board
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child drags loose puzzle pieces, rotating them when needed, to completely fill a target silhouette.
interaction: Drag each piece from the tray into the outline; a piece snaps into place when it is close and correctly oriented. A selected piece is rotated with a rotate handle or tap (snaps 45 degrees) and flipped for older bands. The item auto-submits when the silhouette is fully covered, or the child taps DONE; partial fills are scored by the fraction of area correctly placed.
self_teach: A ghost-hand drags one piece into the outline and it snaps with a click; a two-piece warm-up requiring no rotation precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Spatial assembly ('form board') is a distinct, strong marker of the visualization factor
learning_science.why: Composing parts into a whole taps figure-ground segmentation and mental transformation beyond simple perception.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use loose draggable pieces that fill a silhouette (a digital form board) rather than a 'which pieces fit' multiple-choice picture.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Manual for Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Form Board (VZ) marker tests.

learning_science.principle: Manipulatives externalize spatial reasoning and reduce working-memory load
learning_science.why: Physically moving pieces lets a child test partial solutions instead of holding them in mind, widening who can demonstrate the skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Allow free rearrangement and undo with snap-to slots so exploration is cheap and only strategy, not memory, is taxed.
learning_science.source: Newcombe (2010), American Educator 34(2):29-35, 'Picture this: increasing math and science learning by improving spatial thinking'.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial-area credit (M-POLY) plus placement efficiency (M-EFF: pieces placed vs re-dragged) and the placement sequence (M-PATH) turn one silhouette into a rich curve; strong solvers place large anchor pieces first and finish with few re-drags, so near-optimal assembly of a hard multi-piece silhouette at speed separates the tail even when several children all reach full coverage.
age_rationale: K-1 gets 2-3 large pieces, no rotation required, and a generous snap radius; 2-3 needs simple 90-degree rotations; 4-5 adds 45-degree rotations and more pieces; 6-8 uses 6-9 tangram pieces requiring rotation and reflection. Fine placement is removed by snapping so success reflects visualization rather than dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: 2-piece slide-together (K-1) to 9-piece rotate-and-reflect tangram silhouettes (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: piece count; rotation/reflection required; snap radius; silhouette ambiguity (multiple valid tilings); interior guide lines on/off
adaptive.notes: Silhouettes and piece sets are generated from a tiling engine, with difficulty set by number of pieces and required transformations; any complete tiling is accepted.

engagement_hook: Classic tangram/puzzle satisfaction: pieces click home and the silhouette lights up when complete, with a 'perfect fit' streak.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor drag precision (snap-to); rotation-control discoverability (ghost-hand shows the rotate handle); silhouettes with multiple valid solutions (accept any complete tiling, score coverage not one key).

name: Plan-the-Path
topics_techniques_covered: mazes_route_planning
one_liner: The child guides a character from start to exit through a maze, and in harder items plans the shortest route that also collects required gems.
interaction: Drag the character, or tap adjacent cells / an arrow pad, to move it cell-by-cell along open corridors; walls block movement. Route-planning items require reaching the exit after collecting all gems, with a live move counter and a 'lock in route' commit for older children. The item completes when the character reaches the exit with all required gems collected.
self_teach: A ghost-hand traces the character smoothly from start through the turns to the exit; one warm-up on a tiny three-turn maze precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Route planning engages look-ahead planning (executive spatial function) beyond simple tracing
learning_science.why: Planning a multi-target shortest path taxes mental simulation of future states, a higher-order spatial component.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Add a plan-before-move, multi-gem, fewest-steps variant and score moves against the optimal path, not just completion.
learning_science.source: Shallice (1982), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298:199-209, 'Specific impairments of planning' (Tower of London paradigm).

learning_science.principle: Mazes are a long-validated child spatial/planning measure requiring foresight and impulse control
learning_science.why: Successful solving requires inhibiting the first move and planning ahead, a documented developmental spatial-executive marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Record first-move latency and dead-end entries as planning-vs-impulsive-tracing indices.
learning_science.source: Porteus (1965), 'Porteus Maze Test: Fifty Years' Application', Pacific Books.

tail_precision_rationale: First-move latency (M-RTFIRST) captures planning before acting, while path efficiency vs optimal (M-EFF) and dead-end re-entries (M-REV) reveal look-ahead depth; at the tail a long reflective pause followed by a near-optimal, backtrack-free route through a dense multi-gem maze (high M-DIFFREACH) is the plan-ahead signature that distinguishes gifted problem-solvers from fast trial-and-error tracers.
age_rationale: K-1 gets a large single-solution maze with few turns and finger-drag movement; 2-3 adds blind alleys; 4-5 introduces shortest-path with 1-2 gems; 6-8 uses dense mazes with multiple required targets and a fewest-steps budget. Wide corridors and snap-to-cell movement keep motor demand low across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: single clear path with few turns (K-1) to dense multi-gem shortest-path planning under a move budget (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; corridor branching / dead-ends; number of required gems; move budget vs optimal; plan-first (no free retrace) mode
adaptive.notes: Mazes are generated procedurally (DFS/Prim) with guaranteed solvability and a computed optimal-path length, so difficulty and the optimum for M-EFF scoring are known for every clone.

engagement_hook: A friendly character to steer, gems to grab, and 'stars for fewest steps' turn planning into a mini adventure.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (both drag and tap allowed, wide corridors); reading (none, fully wordless); rewarding speed over planning (credit efficiency and optimality, not raw time).

name: Build-the-Blocks
topics_techniques_covered: block_design
form_board
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child reproduces a shown pattern by placing and rotating colored blocks into a grid (2D block design), scaling up to building a 3D model from a blueprint.
interaction: Drag tiles from a palette into grid cells; each tile can be rotated (tap or handle, snaps 90 degrees) and tiles include solid colors and diagonal two-color splits (classic block design). The grid cell snaps the tile in. For 6-8 the child instead builds a stack of unit cubes on an isometric board to match given front/side/top views. Scoring matches each cell or voxel to the target; DONE submits.
self_teach: A ghost-hand drags a tile in, rotates it once to match the card, and it snaps; a two-cell warm-up with solid colors only precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Block Design is a premier measure of visuospatial analysis (part-whole decomposition)
learning_science.why: Reconstructing a design requires segmenting the whole into block-sized units and mapping each block's orientation, a core spatial-analytic skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use rotatable diagonal-split tiles and score per-cell match so the task captures decomposition and orientation, not color memory.
learning_science.source: Wechsler (2014), WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual, Block Design subtest; Kohs (1920), Journal of Educational Psychology, 'The Block-Design Tests'.

learning_science.principle: Constructing to a target ('copy the model') externalizes spatial visualization linked to STEM
learning_science.why: Building tasks tap and predict the spatial skills that forecast later STEM achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an isometric build-to-blueprint variant for older bands to extend the range into 3D construction.
learning_science.source: Wai, Lubinski & Benbow (2009), Journal of Educational Psychology 101(4):817-835, 'Spatial ability for STEM domains: aligning over 50 years of cumulative psychological knowledge'.

tail_precision_rationale: Per-cell partial credit (M-POLY) with build trajectory (M-PROG) and rotation/placement efficiency (M-EFF, M-PATH) expose strategy: tail solvers decompose the design and place each block in near-minimal moves without churn (low M-REV). Reproducing a hard diagonal-split design or a 3D blueprint at speed with an efficient move path (high M-DIFFREACH) grades the top of the distribution beyond a right/wrong final score.
age_rationale: K-1 uses a 2x2 grid of solid-color tiles, no rotation, and big snap cells; 2-3 adds 90-degree rotation of diagonal tiles on a 2x2; 4-5 uses 3x3 designs; 6-8 uses 3x3+ designs and a 3D build-to-orthographic-views task. Snapping into cells removes placement dexterity so scores reflect analysis rather than aim.

adaptive.content_range: 2x2 solid-color copy (K-1) to 3x3 diagonal-split designs and 3D voxel build-to-blueprint (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; presence of diagonal-split tiles; rotations required; number of colors; 2D vs 3D (orthographic-view) target; time pressure
adaptive.notes: Target designs are generated by sampling a tile and rotation per cell; 3D targets are generated as voxel sets rendered to three orthographic views, giving unlimited matched clones.

engagement_hook: Tactile 'click the block in' building with a live match-meter that fills as the design comes together; Lego-like flow.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap cells); color vision (use distinct hue plus value or add patterns); rotation discoverability (ghost-hand demonstrates); device screen size for 3x3 grids.

name: Fold-the-Net
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_visualization
paper_folding
one_liner: The child folds a flat net up into a 3D box and works out which face ends up opposite a marked face.
interaction: The child scrubs a 'fold' slider (or taps FOLD) to animate the flat net closing into a 3D cube, then drags to rotate the finished cube in 3D to inspect all faces. To answer, the child taps the color/symbol swatch that is OPPOSITE the marked star face and taps LOCK. A multiple-choice net-to-solid matching variant (pick which cube the net makes) is offered as an alternate shell.
self_teach: A ghost-hand pushes the fold slider so the net closes into a cube and spins it once; a warm-up on a simple cube with an obvious opposite face precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Surface development (net folding) is a classic spatial-visualization factor test
learning_science.why: Mentally folding a 2D net into a 3D solid is a canonical marker of the visualization factor (VZ).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an actual fold animation the child controls plus free 3D rotation, then ask for the opposite or adjacent face.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Surface Development (VZ-3).

learning_science.principle: Interactive 3D exploration supports mental-model construction better than static pictures
learning_science.why: Folding and rotating lets a child build and check an internal 3D model, especially those with weaker static imagery.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Let the child scrub the fold and orbit the cube so exploration behavior itself becomes an observable strategy signal.
learning_science.source: Hegarty (2004), Learning and Instruction 14(3):343-351, 'Dynamic visualizations and learning: getting to the difficult questions'.

tail_precision_rationale: Exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE: how much the child scrubs the fold and orbits the cube) plus error type (M-ERRTYPE: adjacent-face near-miss vs random) reveal whether a correct answer came from a solid mental model or from manipulation-by-trial; tail solvers answer hard nets (more faces, asymmetric symbols) correctly with minimal orbiting (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE), indicating internal visualization rather than externalized search.
age_rationale: Mentally mapping a 2D net to a 3D solid exceeds most K-1 children (pre-operational limits on cross-dimensional transformation), so the type starts at 2-3 with a simple six-square cube and an obvious opposite face; 4-5 adds symbols on faces; 6-8 uses irregular nets, prisms/pyramids, and adjacency (not just opposite) questions. The controllable fold animation scaffolds younger children without giving away the answer.

adaptive.content_range: simple cube net, name the opposite face (2-3) to irregular prism nets with adjacency questions and multiple candidate solids (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: net regularity; solid type (cube to prism/pyramid); symbol vs color faces; opposite vs adjacent question; number of multiple-choice candidate solids; fold-scaffold on/off
adaptive.notes: Nets are generated from valid unfoldings of a chosen solid with a fixed face-adjacency map, so the correct opposite/adjacent face is computed automatically for any clone.

engagement_hook: Watching a flat cross fold itself into a box you can spin in your hands is inherently delightful; 'origami you control'.
construct_irrelevant_risks: 3D rotation control on touch (large orbit area, momentum off); animation giving away the answer (fold stops before revealing hidden faces unless the child chooses to orbit); symbol legibility.

name: Fold & Punch
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
one_liner: The child folds a paper one or more times, punches a hole, then predicts where all the holes will be once it is unfolded.
interaction: The child taps fold controls (fold left/right, top/bottom, or a diagonal for older) to animate the sheet folding, then taps a spot to punch a hole through all layers (shown on the folded stack). The child predicts the result by tapping cells on the unfolded grid where holes will appear, then taps CHECK/LOCK. In warm-up the sheet actually unfolds to reveal the truth; in scored items the child commits predictions first.
self_teach: A ghost-hand folds the sheet once, punches, then unfolds to show the two symmetric holes; one warm-up (single fold, one punch) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Paper folding with punched holes is a benchmark spatial-visualization test
learning_science.why: Predicting the unfolded hole pattern requires mentally reversing folds and applying reflection symmetry, a core visualization operation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child perform the folds and punches, then mark predicted holes on the unfolded grid as a constructed response rather than a four-option pick.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Paper Folding (VZ-2).

learning_science.principle: A single wordless worked demonstration teaches a novel spatial rule faster than instructions (worked-example effect)
learning_science.why: Worked examples reduce cognitive load for novices, so the unfold-reveal teaches the reflection rule without text.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The warm-up performs one full fold-punch-unfold as a wordless worked example, then scored items withhold the reveal until after commit.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3):251-296, 'Cognitive architecture and instructional design' (worked-example effect).

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring predicted-vs-true holes as graded overlap (M-POLY) and classifying misses (M-ERRTYPE: correct hole count but wrong reflection axis is a systematic near-miss vs random) extracts fine tail information from one item; the sharpest separator is accuracy on multi-fold, asymmetric-punch items (high M-DIFFREACH) where each extra fold doubles the required reflections, so able children track all layers while others lose a fold.
age_rationale: Reversing folds by reflection is beyond most K-1 children, so the type begins at 2-3 with a single fold and one punch on a coarse grid; 4-5 uses two orthogonal folds; 6-8 uses three folds including an oblique fold and multiple punches. Tapping large grid cells keeps motor demand minimal, and the live unfold in warm-up scaffolds the rule.

adaptive.content_range: single fold plus one punch on a 4x4 grid (2-3) to three folds including an oblique fold with multiple punches on a fine grid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of folds; fold orientation (orthogonal vs oblique); number and position of punches; grid resolution; symmetric vs asymmetric layout
adaptive.notes: A fold sequence plus punch coordinates define the item; the true unfolded hole set is computed by reflecting punches across each fold axis in reverse order, so every clone is auto-keyed and partial credit is exact.

engagement_hook: Hands-on 'fold the paper, punch it, guess the surprise' with a satisfying unfold reveal; like a magic trick the child performs.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large grid taps); giving away the rule (reveal only in warm-up or after commit); grid-resolution ambiguity (snap punches to cell centers).

name: What Do They See
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
one_liner: The child figures out what a character sees from where it stands, by moving the character or pointing a dial toward a target from the character's viewpoint.
interaction: A small scene of labeled objects is shown from above with a character token. As the child drags the character around the scene (snapping to set viewpoints), a live 'what they see' strip updates, showing the objects in the character's left-to-right order. To answer, the child either drags the character to the spot that would produce a shown view, or (older bands) rotates a pointer dial to indicate the direction to a hidden target as seen from the character's heading, then taps LOCK.
self_teach: A ghost-hand walks the character to the other side and the 'what they see' strip flips left-to-right; a warm-up asks the child to match one simple two-object view before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Perspective taking (spatial orientation) is a spatial factor dissociable from object rotation
learning_science.why: Imagining a scene from another viewpoint (self-to-object) is separable from mentally rotating objects and predicts navigation ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score directional/heading error to a target from an imagined viewpoint, not object rotation, to isolate the perspective factor.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov & Hegarty (2001), Memory & Cognition 29(5):745-756, 'A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability'.

learning_science.principle: Young children default to their own view (egocentrism) and improve with concrete, movable viewpoints
learning_science.why: The three-mountains work shows perspective taking develops later, and letting children move a character scaffolds the viewpoint shift.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a live, movable character and start with 2-4 discrete viewpoints for younger bands rather than abstract heading estimation.
learning_science.source: Piaget & Inhelder (1956), 'The Child's Conception of Space' (three-mountains task), Routledge & Kegan Paul.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Perspective-taking angular error
new_measurements_proposed.what: Signed angular error between the child's indicated heading/direction and the true direction to the target from an imagined viewpoint.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Grades perspective responses far more finely than right/wrong, and its systematic component quantifies residual egocentric bias; low angular error at large viewpoint offsets is a navigation-linked tail signal standard batteries omit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On pointing/heading items, record the dial angle and subtract the geometric correct heading; decompose into random and egocentric-bias components.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=10 pointing trials across a range of viewpoint offsets for a stable error and bias estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: Continuous heading/pointing error (M-VIEWANG) grades responses far more finely than right/wrong, and its systematic component (pointing as if from the child's own position) quantifies residual egocentric bias; at the tail, low angular error on large viewpoint offsets (>=135 degrees) with little exploration (M-EXPLORE) marks children with a true allocentric model, a navigation-linked spatial strength standard batteries omit.
age_rationale: Robust allocentric perspective taking emerges around ages 6-8, so the type starts at 2-3 with only 2-4 discrete viewpoints and a live-updating view strip (recognition, not generation); 4-5 uses more objects and 4-8 viewpoints; 6-8 uses continuous pointing-dial heading estimation. The movable character gives concrete support so younger children are not blocked by pure imagery, and K-1 is excluded because egocentric responding dominates.

adaptive.content_range: match a two-object view among 2-4 viewpoints (2-3) to continuous dial heading toward a target from an imagined orientation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; number and spacing of viewpoints; discrete match vs continuous pointing; viewpoint offset magnitude; self vs array reference frame
adaptive.notes: Scenes are generated by placing N labeled objects at coordinates and the correct view/heading is computed geometrically, so items and keys clone automatically; works_well is 'med' because the construct's onset is late and floor effects appear before about age 6.

engagement_hook: A character with a live 'camera view' you control: move it around and watch the world reorder from its eyes; it feels like directing a scene.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor for young bands (report reliability, exclude K-1); reading (labels replaced by icons); motor (snap viewpoints, coarse dial detents for younger); mistaking left/right mirroring for error (score angular direction consistently).

name: Slice-It
topics_techniques_covered: cross_sections
one_liner: The child slides a cutting plane through a 3D solid and picks the 2D shape revealed at the cut.
interaction: A rotatable 3D solid is shown; the child drags a cutting-plane slider to move the slice up and down (and, for older bands, drags a tilt handle to angle the plane). A live outline previews where the plane meets the solid; the child then taps the matching 2D cross-section shape from an option row and taps LOCK. A concrete variant 'cuts' a familiar object (carrot, apple) and asks for the cut face.
self_teach: A ghost-hand slides the plane through a cylinder and taps the circle; a warm-up with a straight cut of a familiar object precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Cross-sectioning (penetrative thinking) is a spatial skill central to STEM
learning_science.why: Inferring the internal 2D shape of a 3D solid predicts and supports learning in geology, anatomy, and engineering, and is trainable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an interactive slice-and-reveal with adjustable plane height and angle rather than a single static picture.
learning_science.source: Cohen & Hegarty (2012), Learning and Individual Differences 22(6):868-874, 'Inferring cross sections: when internal visualizations are more important than properties of external visualizations'.

learning_science.principle: Dynamic, interactive visualization aids those with lower spatial imagery
learning_science.why: Moving the cutting plane supports building the internal model instead of requiring it in advance.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a movable plane and rotatable solid and log how much the child explores before committing.
learning_science.source: Hegarty (2004), Learning and Instruction 14(3):343-351, 'Dynamic visualizations and learning: getting to the difficult questions'.

tail_precision_rationale: Exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE: plane moves and rotations sampled) and near-miss error typing (M-ERRTYPE: circle-for-ellipse on an oblique cut, or triangle-for-trapezoid) distinguish children who read the geometry from those who guess the 'obvious' shape; the tail signal is correct oblique cross-sections of prisms and cones (high M-DIFFREACH) answered with minimal plane-scrubbing, indicating internal penetrative visualization.
age_rationale: Predicting internal cross-sections is difficult before about age 9 and keeps improving through adolescence, so the type is scoped to 4-5 (concrete objects, straight axis-aligned cuts, few options) and 6-8 (abstract solids including prisms, cones, and pyramids with oblique cuts). It is excluded from K-1 and 2-3 because penetrative thinking is largely undeveloped and would floor.

adaptive.content_range: straight cut of a familiar object or cylinder, pick among 2-3 shapes (4-5) to oblique cuts of prisms, cones, and pyramids among close distractors (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: solid type; plane orientation (axis-aligned vs oblique); option-set similarity; concrete vs abstract solid; tilt control enabled
adaptive.notes: The correct cross-section is computed analytically per solid-and-plane pair for a library of solids; oblique and irregular solids require more authoring, hence medium cloneability.

engagement_hook: Slice through objects like a knife through fruit and watch the cut face appear; a 'reveal the hidden shape' mechanic that begs experimentation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (scope to 4-5 and up); 3D rendering legibility (clear edges, controllable rotation); plane-control discoverability (ghost-hand); distractor similarity tuned so guessing is penalized.

name: Same Turn or Mirror?
topics_techniques_covered: mental_rotation
one_liner: Two figures appear side by side at some angle apart; the child decides fast whether the second is the SAME shape just turned or a flipped mirror twin.
interaction: Two figures are shown at a set angular disparity. The child taps the big SAME button if the right figure is the left one purely rotated, or the DIFFERENT (mirror) button if it is a reflected twin; the tap is the submission (no separate lock) so response time is clean. Warm-up lets the child drag either figure to spin it and physically check before the timed judgments begin; a young-band shell uses a familiar animal turned versus its mirror.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand spins the right figure until it overlaps the left one (SAME, green chime), then swaps in a mirror twin that never lines up no matter how it spins (DIFFERENT, buzz); one unscored warm-up pair with drag-to-check precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Mental rotation is an analog transformation whose time scales with angle (chronometric same/different)
learning_science.why: In the classic paradigm, same/different reaction time rises linearly with the angular disparity between two figures, so a speeded pair judgment measures the rate of internal rotation directly.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present matched SAME pairs across several angular disparities and regress correct reaction time on angle to estimate each child's rotation rate.
learning_science.source: Shepard & Metzler (1971), Science 171:701-703, 'Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects'.

learning_science.principle: Signal-detection separates true sensitivity from response bias
learning_science.why: Scoring SAME/DIFFERENT as hits and false alarms yields d-prime, so a cautious child and a guesser near the cut are not scored alike.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Balance SAME and mirror-DIFFERENT trials and compute d-prime plus mirror false-alarm rate rather than raw percent correct.
learning_science.source: Green & Swets (1966), 'Signal Detection Theory and Psychophysics', Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: Because the response is a single speeded tap, the reaction-time-versus-angle slope (M-ROTSLOPE), consistency (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE), and signal-detection sensitivity (M-DPRIME) come out clean; at the gifted cut a shallow slope held at high d-prime with a near-zero mirror false-alarm rate (M-MIRRORFA) and a long accuracy-gated speed streak (M-COMBO) is a hard-to-coach rotation signature that a produce-the-alignment task cannot isolate.
age_rationale: The response is one tap, so even K-1 can participate using 2D familiar animals turned versus their mirror at small disparities with drag-to-check in warm-up; 2-3 adds larger disparities and abstract shapes; 4-5 uses 2D block/letter figures with mirror foils; 6-8 uses 3D Shepard-Metzler figures up to 180 degrees. Tapping one of two big buttons removes fine-motor demand so the score reflects the judgment, not aim.

adaptive.content_range: 2D familiar-animal same-versus-mirror at small angles (K-1) to 3D multi-limb figures at 180 degrees with exact mirror foils (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: angular disparity; 2D versus 3D; number of limbs/segments; mirror-foil similarity; response deadline; proportion of mirror trials
adaptive.notes: Each trial is a base figure plus a rotation matrix and an optional reflection, so matched SAME and mirror-DIFFERENT clones at any disparity are generated automatically and the key is exact.

engagement_hook: Fast 'spot the imposter' twin game: a satisfying green chime for catching a true turn and a gentle buzz for the sneaky mirror, with a speed streak that builds only on correct-and-fast taps.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Impulsive fast-wrong tapping (guarded by M-FALSEALARM and the accuracy-gated M-COMBO so raw speed is never rewarded); device/touch reaction-time offset (normalize within device, use the slope whose intercept absorbs motor latency); mirror-versus-rotation confusion in young children (drag-to-check warm-up); visual crowding of 3D figures (limit limb count).

name: Do the Same Turn
topics_techniques_covered: mental_rotation
spatial_visualization
one_liner: A worked example shows one object turned from A to B; the child then spins a brand-new object so it makes the very same turn.
interaction: The top row shows object A and, after it, object B, the result of a hidden rotation. Below, a new object C sits next to an empty frame. The child drags C to rotate it (snapping to allowed angles) until it shows the same rotation that took A to B, then taps LOCK. There is no ghost outline to line up against, so the child must infer the rotation and apply it. A REPLAY button re-runs the A-to-B animation and counts as a scaffold.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand plays the A-to-B turn, then grabs C and spins it by the same amount into the frame with a green chime; one unscored warm-up (a simple quarter-turn) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Mental rotation is a continuous transformation that can be primed and transferred
learning_science.why: When the direction and extent of a rotation are demonstrated, people mentally carry out the same transformation on a new object, so applying a shown turn measures rotation rather than target-matching.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Demonstrate a rotation on A-to-B and require the child to reproduce that transformation on a different object C, scoring the produced orientation.
learning_science.source: Cooper & Shepard (1973), in Chase (ed.) 'Visual Information Processing', Academic Press, 'Chronometric studies of the rotation of mental images'.

learning_science.principle: Analogical transfer of a demonstrated relation is a hallmark of higher reasoning
learning_science.why: Extracting a transformation from one worked case and mapping it onto a new case indexes relational reasoning beyond rote matching.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Withhold any alignment target so success requires transferring the A-to-B relation, and log replay use as a transfer-scaffold signal.
learning_science.source: Gick & Holyoak (1983), Cognitive Psychology 15:1-38, 'Schema induction and analogical transfer'.

tail_precision_rationale: With no target to snap onto, the produced-angle error, the rotation path (M-PATH), the efficiency of reaching the right orientation (M-EFF), and replay-scaffold use (M-HINT) reveal whether the child truly transferred the rotation; at the tail, applying a large or compound turn to a novel object correctly on the first attempt with no replays (high M-DIFFREACH, zero M-HINT) is a relational-rotation signal that a line-up-to-the-ghost task cannot capture.
age_rationale: Inferring a rotation from a worked example and transferring it to a new object exceeds most K-1 children, so the type starts at 2-3 with single 2D shapes and 90-degree quarter-turns; 4-5 adds 45-degree turns and two-limb figures; 6-8 uses 3D figures and compound turns. Snap-to-angle rotation removes fine-motor demand so the score reflects the transferred rotation, and K-1 is excluded because relational transfer is not yet reliable.

adaptive.content_range: apply a quarter-turn to a 2D shape (2-3) to apply a compound 3D rotation to a novel multi-limb figure (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: rotation magnitude; single versus compound axis; 2D versus 3D object; object complexity; snap granularity; replay availability
adaptive.notes: An item is a base object plus a rotation matrix applied to A and, independently, to C; the keyed C orientation is computed from the same matrix, so unlimited matched clones exist at any difficulty.

engagement_hook: A 'copy the magic turn' challenge: watch an object do a trick spin, then make your own object do the exact same trick and lock it with a satisfying click.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor control (snap-to-angle, large drag area); giving away the answer (no alignment ghost; replay shows only A-to-B, never C's target); over-reliance on replay (counted as a scaffold via M-HINT); device rotation feel (normalize reaction time within device).

name: Place the Slice
topics_techniques_covered: cross_sections
spatial_visualization
one_liner: Given the exact 2D shape wanted, the child positions and tilts a cutting plane through a 3D solid so the cut face becomes that shape.
interaction: A target 2D shape (for example a hexagon or an oval) is shown. The child drags a height slider to move a cutting plane up and down through a rotatable solid and, for older bands, drags a tilt handle to angle it; a live outline previews the current cut face. When the previewed cut matches the target the child taps LOCK. Partial credit is given for how closely the produced cross-section matches the target. An alternate 'build the cut' shell has the child place vertices to draw the resulting cross-section polygon.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand tilts the plane through a cube until the preview outline morphs into the shown hexagon and snaps green; one unscored warm-up (make a square from a straight cut of a cube) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Cross-sectioning (penetrative thinking) is a trainable STEM-linked spatial skill
learning_science.why: Inferring how a plane meets a solid underlies geology, anatomy, and engineering and is separable from other spatial factors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an interactive plane whose height and tilt the child controls, and require producing a named cross-section rather than only recognizing one.
learning_science.source: Cohen & Hegarty (2012), Learning and Individual Differences 22(6):868-874, 'Inferring cross sections: when internal visualizations are more important than properties of external visualizations'.

learning_science.principle: Generating a solution produces stronger, more diagnostic performance than recognizing one (generation effect)
learning_science.why: Requiring the child to construct the cut plane, rather than pick from options, taxes and reveals the internal model more fully and resists guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Make the response an inverse construction (set the plane to hit a target shape) scored by continuous match, not a four-option choice.
learning_science.source: Slamecka & Graf (1978), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory 4(6):592-604, 'The generation effect: delineation of a phenomenon'.

tail_precision_rationale: Continuous match of the produced cross-section (M-POLY) plus plane-adjustment efficiency (M-EFF) and exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE) turn one inverse item into a graded curve; the tail signal is producing a hard oblique cross-section (a hexagon from a cube, an ellipse from a cone) with few plane moves and near-zero placement error (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE), evidence of an internal penetrative model rather than scrub-until-it-looks-right search.
age_rationale: Predicting and producing internal cross-sections is difficult before about age 9 and keeps improving through adolescence, so the type is scoped to 4-5 (familiar solids, straight axis-aligned targets like circle and square, tilt disabled) and 6-8 (prisms, cones, pyramids with oblique targets like ellipse, rectangle, and hexagon, tilt enabled). It is excluded from K-1 and 2-3 because penetrative thinking is largely undeveloped and would floor.

adaptive.content_range: make a circle or square with a straight cut of a familiar solid (4-5) to make a hexagon or ellipse with an oblique cut of a prism, cone, or pyramid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: target-shape difficulty; solid type; tilt enabled or disabled; match tolerance; number of plane degrees of freedom; distance from the obvious axis-aligned cut
adaptive.notes: For a library of solids the set of achievable cross-sections and the plane parameters that yield each are precomputed, so target shapes and their keyed plane placements clone automatically; oblique and irregular solids need more authoring, hence medium cloneability.

engagement_hook: A 'carve it to order' puzzle: you are handed the shape you must reveal, then tilt and slide the knife through the solid until the hidden face pops out exactly right.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (scoped to 4-5 and up); 3D rendering legibility (clear edges, controllable rotation); plane-control discoverability (ghost-hand demo); rewarding blind scrubbing (credit efficiency M-EFF and low exploration, not time); match tolerance tuned so a rough placement does not score as exact.

name: Fold & Overlap
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
spatial_visualization
one_liner: A see-through sheet with printed shapes is folded over; the child predicts the combined pattern where the folded flap lands on the other half.
interaction: A grid sheet shows printed marks on one half and a dotted fold line. The child taps or scrubs a fold control to fold the marked flap over onto the other half; because the sheet is see-through, the flap's marks land mirrored on top of the base marks. To answer, the child taps the cells of the folded footprint where a mark (or a doubled overlap) will appear, then taps CHECK. In warm-up the sheet actually folds to reveal the truth; in scored items the child commits the predicted overlay first.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand folds the flap over and the marks slide across the fold line and stack up, some landing on empty cells and some doubling on existing marks; one warm-up (single fold, two marks) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Mental folding is a distinct spatial transformation, separable from mental rotation
learning_science.why: Folding one part of a figure onto another and tracking where features land is its own transformation with its own developmental trajectory, so it deserves a dedicated item type.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ask the child to predict where surface marks superimpose after a fold (the folded overlay), isolating folding rather than hole-through-layers or net-to-solid reasoning.
learning_science.source: Harris, Newcombe & Hirsh-Pasek (2013), Cognitive Processing 14(2):105-115, 'A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: mental paper folding in young children'.

learning_science.principle: Predicting a superimposed result requires applying reflection symmetry across the fold
learning_science.why: The flap's marks map to their mirror positions across the fold line, so the task exercises reflective mapping and part-to-part correspondence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the predicted overlay against the reflected union of marks, and type near-misses (right count, wrong axis) versus random errors.
learning_science.source: Newcombe & Shipley (2015), in Gero (ed.) 'Studying Visual and Spatial Reasoning for Design Creativity', Springer, 'Thinking about spatial thinking: new typology, new assessments'.

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring predicted-versus-true overlaid cells as graded overlap (M-POLY) and typing misses (M-ERRTYPE: correct overlap count but reflected across the wrong axis is a systematic near-miss versus random) extracts fine tail information from one item; the sharpest separator is accuracy on multi-fold, asymmetric-mark items (high M-DIFFREACH) where each fold adds another reflected superimposition, so able children track every landing while others lose a layer.
age_rationale: Reflecting marks across a fold is beyond most K-1 children, so the type begins at 2-3 with a single fold and two marks on a coarse grid; 4-5 uses two orthogonal folds and doubled-overlap cells; 6-8 adds an oblique fold and denser marks. Tapping large grid cells keeps motor demand minimal, and the live fold in warm-up scaffolds the reflection rule without giving away scored answers.

adaptive.content_range: single fold with two marks on a 4x4 grid (2-3) to two or three folds including an oblique fold with doubled overlaps on a fine grid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of folds; fold orientation (orthogonal versus oblique); number and placement of marks; whether overlaps double; grid resolution; symmetric versus asymmetric layout
adaptive.notes: A fold sequence plus mark coordinates define the item; the true overlay is computed by reflecting marks across each fold axis and unioning onto the folded footprint, so every clone is auto-keyed and partial credit is exact.

engagement_hook: Like folding a painted piece of tracing paper and guessing the picture it makes: marks glide across the crease and stack into a new pattern with a satisfying overlay reveal.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large grid taps); giving away the rule (reveal only in warm-up or after commit); grid-resolution ambiguity (snap marks to cell centers); confusing overlap-doubling with a single mark (use a distinct doubled-cell color and score both).

name: Find the Missing Piece
topics_techniques_covered: form_board
spatial_visualization
one_liner: An outline is almost filled except for one empty gap; the child finds and drops in the single loose piece that fills the gap exactly.
interaction: A target outline is shown mostly filled, leaving one clearly shaped gap. A tray offers several candidate pieces, including mirror and wrong-rotation look-alikes. The child drags the piece they think fits toward the gap; the selected piece can be rotated (snap) and, for older bands, flipped. A correct piece in the correct orientation snaps into the gap and completes the outline; the child taps DONE, or the fit auto-submits on a clean snap. Only one candidate truly completes the gap.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand lifts the matching piece from the tray, rotates it once, and drops it into the gap with a green completion glow, while a mirror look-alike is shown not fitting; one warm-up (a two-piece gap, no rotation) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Form-board part-whole fitting is a classic marker of the spatial (space) factor
learning_science.why: Judging which piece completes a whole taps figure-ground segmentation and mental transformation, the core of the form-board tradition.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require selecting and orienting the single complementary piece for a gap rather than tiling a whole silhouette, isolating complementary-shape reasoning.
learning_science.source: Thurstone (1938), 'Primary Mental Abilities', University of Chicago Press (Space factor; Form Board tests).

learning_science.principle: Physically trying pieces (epistemic action) offloads spatial reasoning and widens access
learning_science.why: Letting the child rotate and test candidate pieces externalizes the mental fit check, reducing working-memory load so strategy, not memory, is measured.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Allow free drag, rotate, flip, and undo with snap-to-gap so exploration is cheap and only the fit decision is scored.
learning_science.source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994), Cognitive Science 18(4):513-549, 'On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action'.

tail_precision_rationale: Candidates sampled before commit (M-EXPLORE), re-drags and re-orients (M-REV, M-EFF), and mirror-versus-rotation error typing (M-ERRTYPE) show whether the child sees the complementary shape at a glance or hunts by trial; at the tail, picking and correctly orienting the right piece for a hard gap with close mirror foils on the first try (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE) marks strong figure-ground and rotation ability beyond a right/wrong score.
age_rationale: Choosing a complementary piece is accessible early, so K-1 uses a large single gap with two or three candidates and no rotation; 2-3 adds 90-degree rotation; 4-5 adds more candidates and 45-degree rotation; 6-8 adds flips and close mirror foils. Snap-to-gap placement removes fine-motor demand so success reflects the fit judgment rather than dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: one large gap with two candidates, no rotation (K-1) to a subtle gap among close mirror and near-rotation foils requiring rotate-and-flip (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: gap shape complexity; number of candidates; rotation and flip required; similarity of mirror/rotation foils; snap tolerance; time pressure
adaptive.notes: A target outline is generated and one piece removed to define the gap; distractors are produced as mirrors, wrong rotations, and near-shapes of the true piece, so matched clones and their key are generated automatically.

engagement_hook: That jigsaw 'aha' of finding the one piece that clicks the picture whole, with a bright completion glow when the outline finally closes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor drag precision (snap-to-gap, large pieces); rotation/flip discoverability (ghost-hand shows the handle); accidental multiple valid pieces (generate exactly one true completion, verify uniqueness); color vision (distinguish pieces by shape not hue).

name: What the Robot Sees
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
spatial_visualization
one_liner: A robot sits at one side of a little scene; the child rebuilds what the robot sees by ordering the objects left-to-right from the robot's point of view.
interaction: A scene of a few distinct objects is shown from above with a robot token on one side. The child reconstructs the robot's view by dragging object cards into a 'what the robot sees' strip in the correct left-to-right order (and, for older bands, marking which object looks nearest). Dragging the robot to a new side updates nothing automatically in scored items, so the child must imagine the view. The child taps LOCK to submit the ordered strip; partial credit is given for correctly ordered pairs.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand walks the robot to a side and then slots the object cards into the strip in the order the robot sees them, flipping left-and-right versus the top-down map; one warm-up (two objects) with a live-updating strip precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Level-2 perspective taking (how a scene looks from another viewpoint) is a distinct developmental milestone
learning_science.why: Beyond knowing what another can see, reconstructing how objects are arranged from someone else's viewpoint requires a genuine viewpoint transformation that emerges in childhood.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child produce the seen left-to-right ordering from the robot's viewpoint, isolating appearance/arrangement (Level-2) rather than mere visibility (Level-1).
learning_science.source: Masangkay, McCluskey, McIntyre, Sims-Knight, Vaughn & Flavell (1974), Child Development 45(2):357-366, 'The early development of inferences about the visual percepts of others'.

learning_science.principle: Concrete, movable scenes scaffold the viewpoint shift and reduce egocentric error
learning_science.why: Young children default to their own view; a movable robot and draggable cards let them build the other viewpoint concretely instead of holding it purely in imagery.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a live-updating strip in warm-up and discrete viewpoints, then withhold the live update in scored items so the ordering must be imagined.
learning_science.source: Newcombe & Huttenlocher (1992), Developmental Psychology 28(4):635-643, 'Children's early ability to solve perspective-taking problems'.

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring the produced ordering as correctly ordered pairs (M-POLY) and typing errors (M-ERRTYPE: a clean left-right reversal is an egocentric near-miss versus a scrambled random order) grades perspective responses far more finely than right/wrong; at the tail, correct orderings from opposite and side viewpoints (large offsets) with little card-shuffling (low M-EXPLORE, high M-DIFFREACH) mark a true allocentric model rather than reading off the child's own view.
age_rationale: Robust other-viewpoint reconstruction emerges around ages 6-8, so the type starts at 2-3 with two objects and a live-updating strip (recognition support); 4-5 uses three objects and side viewpoints; 6-8 uses four or more objects, opposite and diagonal viewpoints, and a near/far judgment. Draggable cards give concrete support so younger children are not blocked by pure imagery, and K-1 is excluded because egocentric responding dominates.

adaptive.content_range: order two objects from a side view with a live strip (2-3) to order four or more objects from an opposite or diagonal viewpoint with a near/far mark (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; viewpoint offset (same side, side, opposite, diagonal); live-updating strip on or off; near/far depth judgment included; object distinctiveness
adaptive.notes: Objects are placed at coordinates and the correct seen ordering from any viewpoint is computed geometrically by projecting onto the robot's left-right axis, so items and keys clone automatically; works_well is medium because the construct's onset is late and floor effects appear before about age 6.

engagement_hook: Become a director seeing through a robot's eyes: walk it around the set and rebuild its shot, with cards clicking into a filmstrip of what it sees.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor for young bands (report reliability, exclude K-1); reading (objects are icons, not words); motor (draggable cards with snap slots); mistaking a consistent left-right reversal for random error (type egocentric reversals separately); over-support (live strip only in warm-up).

name: Cube Turner
topics_techniques_covered: block_design
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child rolls each of several fixed 3D cubes to bring the correct painted face up so the cube tops reproduce a target block-design card.
interaction: A row or grid of 3D cubes sits in fixed slots; each cube has six painted faces (solid colors plus diagonal two-color splits). The child taps a cube's arrow controls (or swipes) to roll it 90 degrees at a time so a chosen face turns to the top, and spins a split face in place to set its diagonal direction. The goal is to make every cube's top face and orientation match the target design card. Scoring compares each cube's top face and orientation to the target; the child taps DONE, or it auto-checks when all tops match.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand rolls one cube until the right color lands on top and, for a split cube, spins it so the diagonal points the right way, snapping green with a chime; one unscored warm-up cube (solid colors, a single roll) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Block Design is a premier measure of visuospatial part-whole analysis
learning_science.why: Reproducing a design requires segmenting the whole into block-sized units and mapping each block's face and orientation, the core spatial-analytic demand.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score each cube's top face and diagonal orientation against the target so the task captures decomposition and orientation rather than color memory.
learning_science.source: Kohs, S. C. (1920). The Block-Design Tests. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 3(5), 357-376.

learning_science.principle: Selecting the correct face of a cube requires mental rotation in depth
learning_science.why: Rolling a cube to bring a hidden face up is an analog rotation in three dimensions, adding an orientation-in-depth demand beyond placing flat tiles.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use real rollable 3D cubes with six painted faces so success requires rotating each cube in depth to find and orient the needed face.
learning_science.source: Shepard, R. N., & Metzler, J. (1971). Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects. Science, 171(3972), 701-703.

tail_precision_rationale: Per-cube partial credit (M-POLY) with the roll sequence (M-PATH) and rolls-versus-minimal efficiency (M-EFF) expose whether a child plans each cube's shortest reorientation or twists blindly (high M-REV); error typing (M-ERRTYPE: right color but wrong diagonal orientation is a systematic near-miss versus a wrong face) plus reproducing a hard nine-cube diagonal design with an efficient, low-churn build (high M-DIFFREACH) grade the top of the distribution beyond a right or wrong final match.
