age_rationale: Rolling a 3D cube while tracking six faces exceeds most K-1 children (and flat-tile block design already serves K-1), so the type starts at 2-3 with solid-color cubes and single 90-degree rolls; 4-5 introduces diagonal two-color faces on a four-cube design; 6-8 uses nine-cube diagonal designs needing multi-step reorientation. Arrow or swipe rolls with snap remove fine-motor demand so scores reflect analysis and depth rotation, not dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: four solid-color cubes with single rolls (2-3) to nine-cube diagonal-split designs needing multi-step reorientation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of cubes; solid versus diagonal-split faces; rolls needed to reach the target face; number of colors; presence of look-alike adjacent faces; time pressure
adaptive.notes: Each cube is a fixed net of six labeled faces and the target is a sampled top-face-and-orientation per cube, so the minimal roll sequence and the key are computed automatically for unlimited matched clones.

engagement_hook: Satisfying 'roll the dice-blocks' tactility: each cube tumbles with a click and snaps green when its face is right, like solving a chunky color-cube puzzle.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (arrow or swipe rolls with snap, large cubes); color vision (distinct hue plus value, or add face patterns); roll-control discoverability (ghost-hand demonstrates rolling and spinning); device screen size for nine-cube designs (scrollable board, generous cube size).

name: Speed Blocks
topics_techniques_covered: block_design
one_liner: The child reproduces a series of colored block designs as fast as they can, earning a speed bonus for each design finished quickly and correctly.
interaction: For each design card the child taps a grid cell to cycle it through the available blocks (solid colors and the four diagonal-split orientations) until the grid matches the card, then taps DONE to bank it and get the next card; a running timer and a speed-bonus meter reward fast, correct completions. A block of several designs is completed against the clock; only fully correct grids score, and speed is credited only on correct designs.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand taps a cell so it cycles color to color to split and lands on the matching block, finishes a small grid, and a speed-bonus star fills; one unscored warm-up design (two cells, no clock) precedes the timed block.

learning_science.principle: Block Design efficiency with time bonuses indexes the speed of visuospatial construction
learning_science.why: Timed completion with bonuses separates children who both analyze and assemble a design quickly from those who are accurate only when untimed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score fully correct designs and credit a speed bonus for fast-correct completions, mirroring the time-bonus scoring of the standard subtest.
learning_science.source: Wechsler, D. (2014). WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual (Block Design subtest, time-bonus scoring). Bloomington, MN: Pearson.

learning_science.principle: Consistency of speeded performance tracks ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule)
learning_science.why: The slowest, most variable responses are more diagnostic than the fastest, so low RT variability at high accuracy is a stronger, less-coachable signal than raw speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Report RT variability and lapses across designs and gate the speed streak on correctness so impulsive fast-but-wrong building is never rewarded.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A 'worst performance' analysis of individual differences. Intelligence, 14(3), 309-325.

tail_precision_rationale: Because designs are completed against a clock, the speed-accuracy operating point (M-SPEEDACC), consistency (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE), and an accuracy-gated speed streak (M-COMBO) come out clean; at the gifted cut, fast completion of hard diagonal designs held at high accuracy with low RT variability and few lapses (high M-DIFFREACH) is a construction-efficiency signature the untimed block-design shell cannot isolate, while M-DRIFT gates fatigue so a slowing late block is not scored as low ability.
age_rationale: Speeded reproduction with a bonus suits ages 4-5 and up (matching the 4-5 colored-cube design item and the 6-8 timed block-design item); 4-5 uses two-by-two solid and simple split designs on a gentle clock, 6-8 uses three-by-three diagonal designs on a tighter clock. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because timing pressure would penalize slow-but-able young builders and confound the score with motor pace. Tap-to-cycle placement removes drag dexterity so the clock measures analysis speed, not aim.

adaptive.content_range: two-by-two solid and simple split designs on a gentle clock (4-5) to three-by-three diagonal designs on a tight clock with speed bonuses (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; diagonal-split presence; time budget and bonus thresholds; number of designs in the block; color count
adaptive.notes: Designs are sampled per cell (color and rotation) with a known key, and the clock and bonus thresholds are parameters, so unlimited matched timed clones exist at any difficulty.

engagement_hook: An arcade 'beat the clock' block race: a bonus star charges when you finish fast and correct, and a combo builds across designs, turning block design into a speed run.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Rewarding impulsive fast-wrong building (only fully correct designs score and the combo is accuracy-gated via M-COMBO and M-ERRTYPE); motor pace confound (tap-to-cycle, large cells, exclude youngest bands); device or touch speed offset (normalize within device); anxiety from timing (gentle clock, encouraging feedback, no penalty for a missed design).

name: Which Way Now?
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
mazes_route_planning
one_liner: Following a marked route through a street map, at each corner the child says whether the traveler turns LEFT or RIGHT from the traveler's own point of view.
interaction: A top-down street map shows a route drawn from start to finish. A car token drives along the route and stops at each corner; the child taps a big LEFT or RIGHT button to say which way the car turns next, from the car's heading (not the map's frame). The car then makes that turn and drives to the next corner. Older bands first plan the route by choosing the shortest legal path before the turn calls begin. The item completes when every turn along the route has been answered.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand rides the car to a corner where the road bends and taps LEFT as the car swings left (green chime), then taps RIGHT at a corner where the car now faces the viewer so the correct answer flips; one unscored warm-up with two easy turns precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Egocentric left-right route decisions measure spatial orientation and perspective taking
learning_science.why: Deciding left or right from a traveler's changing heading requires mentally adopting the traveler's viewpoint, the classic road-map direction-sense task and a marker of spatial orientation distinct from object rotation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ask for left or right relative to the car's current heading (which reverses when the car drives toward the viewer) so an egocentric viewpoint transformation is required, not map-frame reading.
learning_science.source: Money, J., Alexander, D., & Walker, H. T. (1965). A Standardized Road-Map Test of Direction Sense. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press.

learning_science.principle: Route planning is a look-ahead wayfinding task beyond step-by-step tracing
learning_science.why: Choosing and holding a legal shortest route across a network taxes mental simulation of future turns, a planning component of spatial navigation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: For older bands require selecting the shortest legal route before the turn calls begin and score route optimality separately from turn accuracy.
learning_science.source: Wiener, J. M., Buchner, S. J., & Holscher, C. (2009). Taxonomy of human wayfinding tasks: A knowledge-based approach. Spatial Cognition and Computation, 9(2), 152-165.

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring each turn call and typing the errors (M-ERRTYPE: a left-right reversal exactly when the car faces the viewer is a systematic egocentric near-miss versus random) separates children with a true traveler-viewpoint model from those reading the map frame; combined with route optimality (M-EFF, M-PATH) and first-turn planning latency (M-RTFIRST), consistent correct calls on many oncoming turns of a long route (high M-DIFFREACH) is the perspective-plus-planning tail signature a static direction item misses.
age_rationale: Reliable left or right from an imagined changing heading emerges in mid-childhood, so the type starts at 4-5 with a short pre-drawn route and only a few oncoming turns; 6-8 uses long routes with many oncoming turns and adds shortest-route planning before the turn calls. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because egocentric left-right confusion dominates and would floor. Tapping one of two large arrow buttons removes fine-motor demand so the score reflects the viewpoint judgment.

adaptive.content_range: short pre-drawn route with a few turns (4-5) to a long self-planned shortest route with many oncoming (car-facing-the-viewer) turns (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: route length; number of turns; proportion of oncoming (heading-reversed) turns; plan-the-route step on or off; map density
adaptive.notes: A street grid and a route define the item; each turn's correct left or right is computed from the car's heading vector, so turns, keys, and the shortest-route optimum clone automatically; works_well is medium because the construct's onset is mid-childhood and floor effects appear before about age 6.

engagement_hook: A cheerful 'be the co-pilot' driving game: call the turns as the car cruises the streets, with a green chime for each correct call and a little trip-complete celebration.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Left-right labeling ability rather than perspective (use large arrow-marked LEFT and RIGHT buttons and a warm-up to confirm the child knows the buttons); developmental floor for young bands (exclude K-1 and 2-3, report reliability); reading (fully wordless, icon buttons); mistaking a consistent egocentric reversal for random error (type oncoming-turn reversals separately via M-ERRTYPE).

name: Path Connect
topics_techniques_covered: mazes_route_planning
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child rotates road or pipe tiles in a grid so a single connected path links the start to the goal, and in harder items visits required stops in the fewest tiles.
interaction: A grid is seeded with road or pipe tiles (straights, bends, T-pieces, and cross-pieces) in scrambled orientations, plus a fixed START and GOAL. The child taps a tile to rotate it 90 degrees; when the tiles form an unbroken route from start to goal the path lights up and the item completes. Route-planning items add required stop tiles that the single path must pass through, with a live tile-and-rotation counter and a fewest-tiles target for older children.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand taps a bent tile so it rotates and clicks into line, then taps one more so the road connects end to end and lights up with a chime; one unscored warm-up (a two-tile connect) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Building a connected route is a look-ahead planning and constraint-satisfaction task
learning_science.why: Forming one continuous path that satisfies connectivity (and required stops) demands mental simulation of how each tile's orientation propagates the route, a planning component of spatial problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require a single connected start-to-goal path (with required stops for harder items) and score tiles and rotations against the minimal solution rather than mere completion.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 298(1089), 199-209.

learning_science.principle: Orienting each tile requires mental rotation integrated with spatial visualization
learning_science.why: Judging how a bend or T-piece must be turned to accept and pass the route couples rotation with holding the whole path in mind, a core visualization demand.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use rotatable connector tiles so the child must mentally rotate each piece to see how its openings align before committing, and log rotations as a process signal.
learning_science.source: Linn, M. C., & Petersen, A. C. (1985). Emergence and characterization of sex differences in spatial ability: A meta-analysis. Child Development, 56(6), 1479-1498.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial connectivity credit (M-POLY: fraction of the route linked and required stops reached) plus rotations-versus-minimal efficiency (M-EFF) and the rotation sequence (M-PATH, M-EXPLORE) reveal whether a child sees the whole route and turns each tile purposefully or spins tiles at random (high M-REV); solving a dense grid with required stops in near-minimal rotations (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE) is the plan-the-whole-path tail signal beyond a solved or not-solved score.
age_rationale: Rotating a tile to connect two ends is accessible early, so 2-3 uses a tiny grid with a two- or three-tile straight connect; 4-5 adds bends and a longer single path; 6-8 uses a dense grid with T and cross tiles and required stops under a fewest-tiles target. Tap-to-rotate with snapping removes fine-motor demand so success reflects route planning and tile orientation rather than dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: two-to-three tile straight connect (2-3) to a dense grid of bends, T-pieces, and cross-pieces with required stops under a fewest-rotations target (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; tile mix (straights versus bends versus T and cross); number of required stops; minimal-rotation target; number of decoy tiles that must stay unused
adaptive.notes: A solvable board is generated from a known path then tiles are scrambled by random rotation, so the minimal-rotation solution and required-stop key are computed for every clone; connectivity is checked by tracing tile openings.

engagement_hook: That 'click it into line' pipe-puzzle satisfaction: tiles snap as they turn and the whole road lights up and flows when the path finally connects.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (tap-to-rotate with snap, large tiles); rotation discoverability (ghost-hand shows a tile turning); multiple valid solutions (score connectivity and rotation efficiency, accept any minimal-length connected path); rewarding blind spinning (credit M-EFF and low M-EXPLORE, not time or taps).

name: Scan Stacker
topics_techniques_covered: cross_sections
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child scrubs through a stack of 2D cross-section slices (like a medical scan) and works out which 3D solid would produce them.
interaction: A slider scrubs a scan line from the top of a hidden solid to the bottom, showing the 2D cross-section at each height as a stack of slices the child can replay. To answer, the child taps which of several candidate 3D solids would produce that exact sequence of cross-sections and taps LOCK; an alternate 'build it' shell has the child stack sized disks or plates to assemble the solid the slices imply. Distractor solids differ in how a single slice would change (for example a cone versus a cylinder versus a pyramid).
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand scrubs the scan of a cone so the circle slice shrinks from big to a point, then taps the cone among the candidates with a green chime; one unscored warm-up (a cylinder whose circle stays the same size) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Cross-sectioning (penetrative thinking) is a STEM-linked spatial skill
learning_science.why: Relating a solid to its internal planar cross-sections underlies geology, anatomy, and engineering and is separable from other spatial factors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present the full sequence of cross-sections and require inferring the solid, so the child reasons about how the cut face changes with height rather than reading one static picture.
learning_science.source: Cohen, C. A., & Hegarty, M. (2012). Inferring cross sections: When internal visualizations are more important than properties of external visualizations. Learning and Individual Differences, 22(6), 868-874.

learning_science.principle: Integrating a series of slices into a whole is section-to-3D mental synthesis
learning_science.why: Building a 3D model from successive cross-sections is exactly the skill experts use to read medical and geological scans, and it predicts and is supported by spatial training.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child scrub and replay the slice stack and then identify or assemble the implied solid, logging how much scrubbing precedes the commit.
learning_science.source: Hegarty, M., Keehner, M., Khooshabeh, P., & Montello, D. R. (2009). How spatial abilities enhance, and are enhanced by, dental education. Learning and Individual Differences, 19(1), 61-70.

tail_precision_rationale: How much the child scrubs and replays the stack before committing (M-EXPLORE) and near-miss typing (M-ERRTYPE: choosing a cylinder for a cone reads the first slice but not the change, versus a random pick) reveal whether the solid is inferred from the slice progression or guessed from one frame; correctly identifying or assembling hard solids (cones, pyramids, composite shapes) with little scrubbing (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE) marks an internal section-to-3D model, and the build shell adds graded assembly credit (M-POLY).
age_rationale: Penetrative, section-to-solid reasoning largely develops after about age 9 and keeps improving through adolescence, so the type is scoped to 4-5 (familiar solids with clearly changing slices such as a cone versus a cylinder, few candidates) and 6-8 (prisms, pyramids, and composite solids with subtly changing slices and close distractors). K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because the skill is largely undeveloped and would floor. Slider scrubbing and tap-to-pick keep motor demand minimal.

adaptive.content_range: pick among a cone, cylinder, and sphere from clearly changing slices (4-5) to identify or stack-build prisms, pyramids, and composite solids from subtly changing slices (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: solid set and similarity of candidates; how much the slice changes with height; number of candidates; identify versus build-by-stacking response; presence of a composite two-part solid
adaptive.notes: For a library of solids the height-indexed cross-section sequence is precomputed, so slice stacks and keys clone automatically; composite and irregular solids need more authoring, hence medium cloneability.

engagement_hook: Play scan-room detective: scrub a glowing scan up and down through a mystery object and watch the slice morph, then call out what solid is hiding inside.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (scoped to 4-5 and up, report reliability); slice legibility (clear high-contrast slices, replayable stack); slider discoverability (ghost-hand demonstrates scrubbing); distractor similarity tuned so one-frame guessing is penalized (M-ERRTYPE); device screen size for candidate solids (large tappable candidates).

name: Hide from the Seeker
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
one_liner: The child slides a screen or moves a toy so that a character on one side either cannot (or can) see a target object along its line of sight.
interaction: A top-down scene shows a seeker character facing into the scene and a target toy, with a faint sight-ray drawn from the seeker toward the target. The child drags a movable wall/screen into snap slots (or drags the toy to a snap spot) so the ray is broken for HIDE items or clear for SHOW items; the ray turns red when blocked and green when clear. The child taps LOCK to submit. For older bands several seekers are present and the child must hide the toy from all of them at once, or place it where exactly one seeker can see it.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drags the screen across the seeker's sight-ray until the ray snaps and the toy dims, with a chime; one unscored warm-up (one seeker, one screen slot) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Level-1 visual perspective taking (knowing what another can and cannot see) is present in early childhood
learning_science.why: Children reliably judge whether another person can see an object years before they can report how a scene looks from that viewpoint, so a visibility task is developmentally valid at K-1 where appearance tasks floor.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score whether the child blocks or clears the seeker's line of sight (a Level-1 visibility judgment) rather than how the scene looks from the seeker, and begin at K-1 with one seeker.
learning_science.source: Flavell, J. H., Everett, B. A., Croft, K., & Flavell, E. R. (1981). Young children's knowledge about visual perception: Further evidence for the Level 1-Level 2 distinction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 73(1), 99-103.

learning_science.principle: Manipulatives externalize the viewpoint computation and lower working-memory load
learning_science.why: Sliding a real screen lets a child test the line of sight instead of holding it in mind, widening who can demonstrate the skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use draggable snap-to screens and objects with a live sight-ray so exploration is cheap and only the visibility decision is scored.
learning_science.source: Kirsh, D., & Maglio, P. (1994). On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action. Cognitive Science, 18(4), 513-549.

tail_precision_rationale: First-action latency (M-RTFIRST) and exploration (M-EXPLORE: screen positions tried) separate children who see the sight-line at a glance from those who slide-and-check; on hard multi-seeker items where a spot must be hidden from several viewpoints at once (high M-DIFFREACH), placing the block correctly on the first move along an efficient path (M-EFF, M-PATH) marks a child who computes several lines of sight simultaneously, a perspective signal beyond right or wrong.
age_rationale: Level-1 visibility judgments are reliable from about age 3, so the type starts at K-1 with one seeker and one screen slot; 2-3 adds more slots and a movable toy; 4-5 uses several seekers who must all be blocked (or a spot visible to exactly one). It stops at 4-5 because older bands are better served by the harder Level-2 appearance types (SPA-VIEW-01, SPA-SCENE-01, SPA-ROADMAP-01); large snap targets keep motor demand minimal.

adaptive.content_range: one seeker, one screen slot, block the view (K-1) to hiding a toy from several seekers at once or revealing it to exactly one (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of seekers; number of screen and target snap positions; block-all versus reveal-to-one; scene clutter; obliqueness of the sight-line
adaptive.notes: Seeker, target, and obstacle coordinates are sampled and each line-of-sight is computed by segment intersection, so items and the block/clear key clone automatically.

engagement_hook: A playful hide-and-seek: slide the fort wall to hide the treasure from the pirate's gaze, with the sight-beam snapping red the instant the view is blocked.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap-to slots, large drag targets); reading (fully wordless, icon seekers); developmental floor avoided by scoring Level-1 visibility rather than Level-2 appearance; mistaking a partially blocked ray for blocked (require full occlusion within tolerance and show ray color clearly).

name: Snap the Photo
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
one_liner: A camera-character sits on one side of a small scene and the child taps which of several photos shows exactly what that character sees.
interaction: A scene of a few distinct objects is shown from above with a camera-character on one side. Below are three or four candidate photos (front-on views); the child taps the photo matching what the camera sees from its side, then taps LOCK. Distractor photos include the child's own (opposite) view, a left-right mirrored view, and a neighbour-side view. For older bands the camera sits at diagonal positions and more objects are added. In warm-up the chosen photo is checked against a live preview; in scored items the preview is hidden.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand moves the camera to one side, a thought-bubble shows its photo, and the matching option lights green with a chime; one warm-up (two objects, two photos) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Level-2 perspective taking is measurable by recognition before it can be produced
learning_science.why: Children can pick the correct appearance of a scene from another viewpoint earlier than they can generate it, so a photo-choice format extends viewpoint reasoning down to K-1.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a forced choice among photos (recognition) rather than asking the child to build the view, and include an egocentric own-view foil to detect residual self-centering.
learning_science.source: Masangkay, Z. S., McCluskey, K. A., McIntyre, C. W., Sims-Knight, J., Vaughn, B. E., & Flavell, J. H. (1974). The early development of inferences about the visual percepts of others. Child Development, 45(2), 357-366.

learning_science.principle: Designed distractors turn errors into diagnostic information
learning_science.why: An egocentric (opposite-view) foil, a mirror foil, and a neighbour-side foil each reveal a different failure of the viewpoint transformation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Tag each distractor by its error class and log which the child picks so near-misses are typed rather than pooled.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov, M., & Hegarty, M. (2001). A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability. Memory & Cognition, 29(5), 745-756.

tail_precision_rationale: Because the response is one tap, reaction time (M-RT) and error typing (M-ERRTYPE: choosing the opposite own-view is an egocentric near-miss versus a random pick) come out clean; at the tail, correct photo choices from opposite and diagonal camera positions (high M-DIFFREACH) with few option revisits (M-EXPLORE) and well-calibrated confidence (M-CONF) mark a child with a true allocentric model rather than one reading off their own view.
age_rationale: Recognizing another's view is accessible earlier than generating it, so K-1 uses two objects, a side camera, and two photos with an obvious egocentric foil; 2-3 adds objects and a third photo; 4-5 uses opposite and diagonal camera positions with mirror and neighbour-side foils. Tapping a large photo removes motor demand; the type stops at 4-5 because the generative SPA-VIEW-01 and SPA-SCENE-01 types carry the harder 6-8 work.

adaptive.content_range: two objects, side camera, two photos (K-1) to four objects at diagonal or opposite positions with mirror and neighbour foils (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; camera offset (side/opposite/diagonal); number of photo options; distractor classes (egocentric/mirror/neighbour); object distinctiveness
adaptive.notes: Objects are placed at coordinates and each candidate photo is rendered by projecting onto a viewpoint's left-right axis, so the key and the typed distractors clone automatically.

engagement_hook: A photo-booth game: peek through the camera-critter's lens and pick its snapshot, with a shutter-click and green frame when you match its view.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading (icons, no words); motor (large tappable photos); developmental floor (recognition format plus egocentric-foil scoring, report reliability at K-1); guessing (three or more options at older bands and a confidence check); left-right mirror confusion typed separately via M-ERRTYPE.

name: What Is It Looking At?
topics_techniques_covered: perspective_taking
one_liner: A character faces into a ring of objects and the child taps the object directly in its line of sight, or for older bands turns the character to aim at a named target.
interaction: A character token faces a direction inside a ring of objects. For younger bands the child taps the object the character is looking straight at (the one on its forward heading); a forward gaze-arrow is shown in warm-up only. For older bands the child drags to rotate the character (snapping to detents) so it faces a named target, then taps LOCK, and the set heading is scored against the true bearing. Objects are icons so no reading is required.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand shows the character's gaze-arrow sweeping onto an object that lights green with a chime, then the arrow hides and the child taps; one warm-up (three objects, gaze shown) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Computing another agent's line of sight (gaze) is a foundational perspective-taking ability present early
learning_science.why: Inferring where an agent is looking along its forward heading is an early-developing social-spatial skill, valid at K-1, before appearance-based Level-2 reasoning is reliable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: At young bands ask the child to identify the object on the character's forward heading, a direct line-of-sight judgment scored as accuracy.
learning_science.source: Flavell, J. H., Everett, B. A., Croft, K., & Flavell, E. R. (1981). Young children's knowledge about visual perception: Further evidence for the Level 1-Level 2 distinction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 73(1), 99-103.

learning_science.principle: Continuous heading error grades perspective responses more finely than right or wrong
learning_science.why: Turning a character to face a target yields a signed angular error whose systematic part indexes residual egocentric bias.
learning_science.concrete_decision: At older bands score the heading the child sets against the true bearing (M-VIEWANG) rather than a discrete pick.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov, M., & Hegarty, M. (2001). A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability. Memory & Cognition, 29(5), 745-756.

tail_precision_rationale: At young bands, error typing (M-ERRTYPE: tapping the object nearest the child rather than the one on the character's heading is egocentric versus random) separates viewpoint reasoning from proximity guessing; at older bands continuous heading error (M-VIEWANG) grades the top precisely, and low angular error when the character faces away from the child (high M-DIFFREACH) marks a true allocentric heading model.
age_rationale: Identifying where a character looks is accessible at K-1 (tap the object on its forward heading); 2-3 adds more objects and off-centre headings; 4-5 switches to turning the character to face a named target, scored by continuous angular error. Snap detents and large tap targets keep motor demand low. It stops at 4-5 because the 6-8 heading work is carried by SPA-VIEW-01's pointing dial.

adaptive.content_range: tap the object a character looks straight at among three (K-1) to rotating the character to face a named target scored by angular error (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; angular spacing; forward-tap versus rotate-to-face; heading offset from the child's own view; detent granularity
adaptive.notes: Objects on a ring and the character heading are parameterized, so the on-heading object and the true bearing for angular scoring are computed for every clone; works_well is med because allocentric heading onset is mid-childhood.

engagement_hook: A follow-the-look game: spot exactly what the puppy is staring at, then grow up to spin it to eye a hidden treat, with a warm chime when your aim is true.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (Level-1 gaze at young bands, angular at older; report reliability); motor (large taps, snap detents); egocentric proximity confound typed via M-ERRTYPE; reading (icons only).

name: Fold to Shape
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
one_liner: The child folds a square sheet along a shown crease and predicts the outline the paper makes after folding, by choosing or building the resulting silhouette.
interaction: A square sheet with a dotted crease and a fold arrow is shown. The child scrubs a fold slider (or taps FOLD) to animate the flap folding over; to answer, the child taps which of several silhouettes matches the folded outline (younger bands) or drags the folded edges onto a grid to reproduce the shape (older). One fold at K-1, two orthogonal folds at 2-3, a diagonal fold at 4-5. In warm-up the fold completes and the true outline is shown; in scored items the child commits the silhouette first, then taps LOCK.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand pushes the fold slider so a corner folds over and the square becomes a smaller shape that matches one silhouette with a chime; one warm-up (single straight fold) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Dynamic forward mental folding is achievable by young children and precedes the harder unfolding skill
learning_science.why: Predicting the shape after folding a sheet is within reach at K-1, unlike reasoning back from an unfolded punched pattern.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Ask for the resulting outline after a forward fold (not the reverse), starting at K-1 with a single fold.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

learning_science.principle: Surface development and folding is a canonical spatial-visualization (VZ) marker
learning_science.why: Mapping a folded configuration is a core visualization operation on the space factor.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an actual fold animation the child controls plus a silhouette choice so the score reflects the folded result.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, R. B., French, J. W., Harman, H. H., & Dermen, D. (1976). Manual for Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests. Educational Testing Service, Paper Folding (VZ-2).

tail_precision_rationale: Graded silhouette overlap (M-POLY) and error typing (M-ERRTYPE: right number of layers but wrong fold direction is a systematic near-miss versus random) extract tail information from one item; the sharpest separator is accuracy on two-fold and diagonal-fold items (high M-DIFFREACH) where the outline depends on tracking several edges at once.
age_rationale: Forward folding of a single crease is accessible at K-1, so K-1 uses one straight fold and a silhouette choice; 2-3 uses two orthogonal folds; 4-5 adds a diagonal fold and a build-the-outline response. K-1 is included because the task is forward (predict the folded shape), not the reversal reasoning that pushes SPA-PUNCH-01 and SPA-FOLDNET-01 to 2-3 and up. Large taps and snap edges keep motor demand minimal.

adaptive.content_range: single straight fold, pick the silhouette (K-1) to a diagonal fold with a build-the-outline response (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of folds; fold orientation (orthogonal versus diagonal); pick-silhouette versus build-outline; decorated-face tracking; number of options
adaptive.notes: A fold sequence over a square defines the item; the folded outline is computed by reflecting the sheet polygon across each crease, so silhouettes and the key clone automatically and overlap is exact.

engagement_hook: Satisfying fold-the-paper-and-watch-its-shape-change play, with the folded outline snapping to match a silhouette like closing a pop-up card.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (slider scrub or taps, snap edges); giving away the answer (reveal only in warm-up or after commit); ambiguous silhouettes (generate a unique folded outline, verify); confusing decorated-face orientation with shape (score outline shape, keep decoration as an optional harder layer).

name: Butterfly Fold
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
spatial_visualization
one_liner: Half of a symmetric picture is painted on a sheet; the child folds it over the crease and predicts where the paint prints onto the blank half, completing the mirror-symmetric picture.
interaction: A sheet shows a dotted centre crease with coloured marks on one half. The child scrubs or taps the fold so the painted half folds onto the blank half; because the paint transfers, each mark prints at its mirror position across the crease. To answer, the child taps the blank-half cells where paint will land (and doubled cells where a print meets an existing mark for two-crease items), then taps CHECK. A vertical crease at K-1, then horizontal and diagonal creases, and a second fold for 6-8. Warm-up folds and reveals the print; scored items commit first.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand folds the painted half over and the marks stamp mirror-images onto the far half with a soft print sound; one warm-up (one mark, vertical crease) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Reflective symmetry is perceptually salient and usable by young children
learning_science.why: Symmetry about a vertical axis is detected and completed early, making a fold-to-mirror task valid at K-1.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Start with a vertical crease (the most salient symmetry axis) and score the reflected print.
learning_science.source: Bornstein, M. H., Ferdinandsen, K., & Gross, C. G. (1981). Perception of symmetry in infancy. Developmental Psychology, 17(1), 82-86.

learning_science.principle: Mental folding that maps marks across a crease is a reflective transformation distinct from rotation
learning_science.why: Applying an axis reflection to predict where features superimpose is its own visualization operation with its own developmental trajectory.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the predicted print against the reflected union of marks and type wrong-axis near-misses.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

tail_precision_rationale: Graded overlap of predicted versus true print (M-POLY) and error typing (M-ERRTYPE: reflected across the wrong axis versus random) grade responses finely; at the tail, accuracy on diagonal-axis and two-crease prints (high M-DIFFREACH) with little scrubbing (M-EXPLORE) marks a child who applies the reflection internally rather than by trial.
age_rationale: Vertical-axis symmetry completion is accessible at K-1; 2-3 adds horizontal axes and more marks; 4-5 adds diagonal axes and doubled overlaps; 6-8 uses two creases in sequence. K-1 is included because completing a mirror is easier than reversing folds. Large snap cells keep motor demand minimal, and warm-up reveals the print to teach the rule.

adaptive.content_range: one mark, vertical crease (K-1) to two-crease diagonal prints with doubled overlaps (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: axis orientation (vertical/horizontal/diagonal); number of marks; single versus double crease; doubled-overlap cells; grid resolution
adaptive.notes: Marks and creases are parameterized and the print is the reflected union across each crease, so every clone is auto-keyed and partial credit is exact.

engagement_hook: Like the classic fold-the-painted-paper-into-a-butterfly craft: press the halves together and watch the pattern mirror itself into a whole.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large snap cells); giving away the rule (reveal only in warm-up); axis ambiguity (draw the crease boldly); confusing single versus doubled marks (distinct doubled-cell colour, score both).

name: Which Fold Made It?
topics_techniques_covered: paper_folding
one_liner: Shown a paper before and after a single fold, the child works out which crease and direction produced the result by choosing or performing the fold.
interaction: The top shows a decorated square (before) and its folded result (after). Below are candidate fold lines (dotted) with direction arrows; the child taps the one crease-and-direction that turns the before into the after, then taps LOCK. An alternate do-it shell lets the child draw the crease by dragging between two edges and pick a direction, animating to check. Younger bands offer two or three horizontal or vertical creases; older bands add diagonal creases and off-centre folds. A REPLAY of the after-shape counts as a scaffold.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand taps a candidate crease and the before-paper folds along it into the after-shape with a chime, while a wrong crease folds to a different shape; one warm-up (two candidate creases) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Selecting the transformation that produced a result (not just predicting a result) taxes and reveals the internal fold model more fully
learning_science.why: Reasoning backward from a result to its cause is a distinct, more diagnostic demand than forward prediction (generation effect).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Make the response the fold that produced the result (an inverse task) scored against the unique crease-and-direction.
learning_science.source: Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4(6), 592-604.

learning_science.principle: Forward mental folding underlies the inverse judgment and is available in early childhood
learning_science.why: Matching a fold to its outcome relies on the same dynamic folding representation young children already possess.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep single folds and concrete before/after images so K-1 children can reason about the crease.
learning_science.source: Harris, J., Newcombe, N. S., & Hirsh-Pasek, K. (2013). A new twist on studying the development of dynamic spatial transformations: Mental paper folding in young children. Cognitive Processing, 14(2), 105-115.

tail_precision_rationale: Replay-scaffold use (M-HINT) and candidates sampled (M-EXPLORE) show whether the child infers the crease at a glance or hunts; error typing (M-ERRTYPE: correct crease line but wrong fold direction versus a wrong line) plus first-try accuracy on diagonal and off-centre folds with no replays (high M-DIFFREACH, zero M-HINT) is an inverse-folding tail signal.
age_rationale: With concrete before/after pictures and single folds, matching a fold to its result is accessible at K-1 (two candidate creases); 2-3 adds a third candidate and a direction; 4-5 adds diagonal and off-centre creases. K-1 is included because single-fold reasoning with a visible outcome is within reach; large taps keep motor demand low. It caps at 4-5 since multi-fold reversal lives in SPA-PUNCH-01 and SPA-FOLDOVER-01 at higher bands.

adaptive.content_range: two candidate creases, straight fold (K-1) to diagonal and off-centre creases with direction (4-5)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of candidate creases; crease orientation; fold direction included; off-centre folds; replay availability
adaptive.notes: The before polygon, crease, and direction determine the after polygon; distractor creases produce distinct after-shapes, so the unique key clones automatically.

engagement_hook: A reverse-engineer-the-fold puzzle: figure out the secret crease that turned the flat paper into the shape, then watch it fold to confirm.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large tappable creases); over-reliance on replay (counted via M-HINT); ambiguous folds (ensure exactly one crease-and-direction yields the after-shape); reading (icons and arrows only).

name: Builder's Studio
topics_techniques_covered: construction_creativity
mental_rotation
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child builds a model by placing and rotating blocks on a snap grid, matching a target blueprint on scored trials and freely inventing a creation in an open build.
interaction: A palette of blocks (squares, rectangles, and ramps at K-1; unit cubes on an isometric board at older bands) feeds a snap grid. The child drags a block in, taps to rotate it (snaps 90 degrees), and it locks to the nearest cell or voxel; undo and clear are available. Scored trials show a target (a 2D pattern, or for 6-8 orthographic front/side/top views) and score the per-cell match; a final open build-anything trial has an always-visible DONE and no target, logging what the child chooses to make.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drags a block in, rotates it once to match the target, and snaps it green; one warm-up (place two blocks, no rotation) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Block construction predicts and builds the spatial skills linked to mathematics and STEM
learning_science.why: Assembling structures to a model taps part-whole visualization that forecasts later achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use build-to-target trials scored per cell or voxel plus an open build, spanning copy and creation.
learning_science.source: Verdine, B. N., Golinkoff, R. M., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Newcombe, N. S., Filipowicz, A. T., & Chang, A. (2014). Deconstructing building blocks: Preschoolers' spatial assembly performance relates to early mathematical skills. Child Development, 85(3), 1062-1076.

learning_science.principle: Orienting each piece to fit requires mental rotation
learning_science.why: Turning a block to the needed orientation before placing is an analog rotation, so building exercises rotation as well as assembly.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require rotation to complete targets and log rotations and their efficiency as a process signal.
learning_science.source: Shepard, R. N., & Metzler, J. (1971). Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects. Science, 171(3972), 701-703.

learning_science.principle: Open creative production reveals divergent, creative-productive giftedness that keyed items miss
learning_science.why: A free build scored for fluency, originality, and elaboration captures the creativity ring of giftedness and authentic construction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a no-target free build and score it with an anchored consensual rubric plus idea fluency and originality.
learning_science.source: Amabile, T. M. (1982). Social psychology of creativity: A consensual assessment technique. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 43(5), 997-1013.

tail_precision_rationale: Per-cell partial credit (M-POLY) with build trajectory (M-PROG) and rotation/placement efficiency (M-EFF, M-PATH, low M-REV) expose whether a child decomposes a target and places each block in near-minimal moves; reproducing a hard blueprint (high M-DIFFREACH) plus, on the open build, idea fluency, originality, elaboration and rubric quality (M-IDEAFLU, M-ORIG, M-ELAB, M-RUBRIC) with free-choice engagement (M-CHOICE) add a creative-productive axis CogAT lacks, jointly grading the analytic and creative tails.
age_rationale: Snapping blocks into a grid makes construction accessible at K-1 (two or three large solid blocks, no rotation); 2-3 adds 90-degree rotation; 4-5 uses larger 2D targets; 6-8 builds 3D voxel models to orthographic blueprints. Snap-to cells and voxels remove placement dexterity so scores reflect analysis, rotation, and invention rather than aim.

adaptive.content_range: place two or three blocks to copy a simple shape and free-build (K-1) to building a 3D voxel model to front/side/top views plus an open creation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: 2D versus 3D; block count and shape variety; rotation required; blueprint versus orthographic views; open versus targeted; palette size
adaptive.notes: Targets are sampled block-and-rotation per cell (or voxel sets rendered to three views), so unlimited matched build-to-target clones exist; the open build is scored by rubric and fluency, not a key.

engagement_hook: A Lego-like studio: snap and spin blocks to nail the blueprint, then a free build-anything round where your creation is celebrated, with the pull of just one more piece.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap cells and voxels, large blocks); rotation discoverability (ghost-hand shows the rotate tap); open-build scoring subjectivity (anchored rubric plus multiple raters for M-RUBRIC, automatic fluency and originality counts); colour vision (distinguish blocks by shape and pattern, not hue only); device screen size for 3D boards (generous cells, scrollable).

name: Marble Run Maker
topics_techniques_covered: construction_creativity
mazes_route_planning
spatial_visualization
one_liner: The child places and tilts ramps, funnels, and chutes so a dropped marble rolls from the start to the goal, and in harder items collects required stars along the way.
interaction: A board has a fixed marble drop-start and a goal bucket. The child drags track pieces (straight ramps, bends, funnels; catchers for older bands) from a tray onto snap slots and taps to flip or tilt their slope; pressing PLAY drops the marble and it rolls under a simple gravity model along the placed pieces. The run succeeds when the marble reaches the goal; route-planning items add required stars the path must hit and a fewest-pieces target. An open make-your-own-run trial logs free creation, and retry is always available.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drops a ramp into a slot, tilts it toward the goal, and the marble rolls down and into the bucket with a chime; one warm-up (one ramp bridges start to goal) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Constructing a working path to a goal is look-ahead planning and constraint satisfaction
learning_science.why: Arranging pieces so the marble reaches the goal requires simulating the route and satisfying connectivity, a planning demand.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require a working start-to-goal run (with required stars for harder items) scored against a fewest-pieces optimum, not just success.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 298(1089), 199-209.

learning_science.principle: Physical construction play develops spatial reasoning and predicts STEM learning
learning_science.why: Building functional structures engages and strengthens the spatial skills tied to later achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a hands-on build-and-test contraption with an open creative round scored for originality and fluency of working solutions.
learning_science.source: Wai, J., Lubinski, D., & Benbow, C. P. (2009). Spatial ability for STEM domains: Aligning over 50 years of cumulative psychological knowledge. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(4), 817-835.

learning_science.principle: Predicting how each sloped piece redirects the marble is spatial visualization of trajectories
learning_science.why: Judging where a ball exits a tilted ramp couples orientation with mental simulation of motion.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use rotatable slope pieces and log rotations and test-runs as process signals.
learning_science.source: Hegarty, M. (2004). Dynamic visualizations and learning: Getting to the difficult questions. Learning and Instruction, 14(3), 343-351.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial credit for path progress and stars reached (M-POLY), placement efficiency versus the fewest-pieces optimum (M-EFF), and test-run exploration (M-EXPLORE, M-PATH) reveal whether a child plans the whole run or tinkers piece-by-piece (high M-REV); solving a dense multi-star run in near-minimal pieces (high M-DIFFREACH) plus originality, fluency, and rubric quality on the open run (M-IDEAFLU, M-ORIG, M-RUBRIC, M-CHOICE) grade the planning and creative-construction tails together.
age_rationale: With snap slots and one required piece, bridging start to goal is accessible at K-1; 2-3 uses a few ramps and bends; 4-5 adds funnels and one required star; 6-8 uses dense boards with several stars and a fewest-pieces target. Snap-to placement and tap-to-tilt remove dexterity so success reflects route planning and construction, not fine motor control.

adaptive.content_range: one ramp bridges start to goal (K-1) to a dense multi-star run under a fewest-pieces target plus an open build (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: board size; piece variety (ramps/bends/funnels/catchers); number of required stars; fewest-pieces target; number of decoy slots; open versus targeted
adaptive.notes: A solvable board is generated from a known working run then pieces are scrambled or removed, so the fewest-pieces optimum and star key are computed for every clone; the marble path is deterministic under the simple gravity model.

engagement_hook: The irresistible marble-run tinkerer: tilt the ramps, hit PLAY, and cheer as the marble rattles down and plops into the bucket, with beg-to-retry fun.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap slots, tap-to-tilt, large pieces); rewarding blind tinkering (credit efficiency M-EFF and plan-first latency M-RTFIRST, not test-run count); multiple valid runs (score connectivity, stars, and piece efficiency, accept any working run); frustration on failure (unlimited retries, encouraging feedback, and M-CHOICE gauges voluntary persistence).

name: Program the Bot
topics_techniques_covered: mazes_route_planning
construction_creativity
one_liner: The child assembles a short sequence of move commands (a little program) that drives a robot across a grid to the goal, collecting required gems in the fewest steps.
interaction: A grid shows a robot at start, a goal, walls, and (harder) gems. The child builds a command strip by tapping or dragging arrow tiles (up/down/left/right for young bands, forward/turn for older) into an ordered sequence, then presses RUN to watch the robot execute it step by step, stopping if it hits a wall. The child edits the sequence and re-runs until the robot reaches the goal with all gems. Older bands add a step budget, a turn-relative command set, and a repeat/loop tile for simple scripting.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drops three arrow tiles into the strip and presses RUN; the robot steps along them to the goal with a chime; one warm-up (two steps, straight line) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Sequencing move commands to reach a goal is look-ahead route planning
learning_science.why: Composing an ordered plan the robot executes requires simulating the whole route before acting, a planning demand beyond step-by-step tracing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the program against a fewest-steps optimum and the required-gem key, not just arrival.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B, 298(1089), 199-209.

learning_science.principle: Early programming and robotics build sequencing and computational thinking accessible to young children
learning_science.why: Command-sequence tools such as programmable floor robots are used successfully from kindergarten, so a build-a-program route task is valid at K-1.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use tangible arrow tiles and a visible run so K-1 children compose and test a short sequence, adding a loop tile only for older bands.
learning_science.source: Bers, M. U. (2018). Coding as a Playground: Programming and Computational Thinking in the Early Childhood Classroom. New York: Routledge.

tail_precision_rationale: Program length versus the fewest-steps optimum (M-EFF), the command sequence (M-PATH), plan-first latency (M-RTFIRST), and edits and re-runs (M-REV, M-HINT run-and-test uses) reveal whether the child plans the full route or edits reactively; recovering after a crash (M-RESUME) and solving dense multi-gem grids in near-optimal programs on few runs (high M-DIFFREACH) is a plan-and-debug tail signature, while M-PROG tracks partial route completion across runs.
age_rationale: Composing a two or three command sequence with absolute arrows and a visible run is accessible at K-1 (programmable floor robots are used in kindergarten); 2-3 lengthens sequences and adds walls; 4-5 adds gems and a step budget; 6-8 uses turn-relative commands and a repeat/loop tile. Tapping arrow tiles removes fine-motor demand so the score reflects planning, not dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: two or three absolute-arrow steps to the goal (K-1) to turn-relative programs with loops, gems, and a step budget on a dense grid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size and walls; sequence length; absolute versus turn-relative commands; number of gems; step budget; loop tile enabled
adaptive.notes: A grid, walls, and gem set define the item; the fewest-steps program is computed by shortest-path search, so the optimum and key clone automatically; the robot's execution is deterministic.

engagement_hook: A beloved code-the-robot game: line up the arrows, hit RUN, and watch your little bot march to the treasure, tweaking and re-running until it nails the path.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (tap or drag large arrow tiles); reading (icon arrows, no text); rewarding trial-and-error over planning (credit program efficiency M-EFF and plan-first latency, count re-runs via M-HINT); left-right or turn-relative confusion at young bands (use absolute arrows until 6-8); frustration (unlimited edits and re-runs, M-RESUME gauges recovery not penalty).

name: Word Safari
topics_techniques_covered: receptive_vocabulary
one_liner: Hear a spoken word and tap the one of four pictures that shows what it means.
interaction: Four picture tiles appear; a speaker button plays the target word (audio in production; play-button + text caption in this demo). The child taps one tile; the tile locks with a confirming pop. No printed words are read. Word rarity auto-adjusts up/down by a frequency staircase after each answer.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the speaker icon pulses, then a floating hand glides to the correct picture and taps it with a happy pop. Then one unscored warm-up uses an easy high-frequency word; any tap is accepted with gentle feedback before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Pairing a spoken word with candidate pictures lets meaning be verified across verbal and visual codes, removing the reading load that would otherwise confound a young child's vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Prompts are audio; every response is a picture, never a printed word.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

learning_science.why: Vocabulary breadth spans a huge range, so presenting words near the child's current level yields the most information per item and reaches the individual ceiling efficiently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A frequency staircase raises/lowers word rarity (Zipf band) after correct/incorrect answers to locate the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

learning_science.why: For gifted screening, differences in print exposure or language background can masquerade as ability; leveling and lure design isolate the target construct.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors are matched on frequency and tagged as phonological / thematic / category lures so error meaning (M-LURETYPE) is separated from motor or guess noise.
learning_science.source: Haladyna, T. M., & Downing, S. M. (2004). Construct-irrelevant variance in high-stakes testing. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 23(1), 17-27.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Lexical frequency ceiling
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Vocabulary breadth is one of the strongest, most stable verbal-ability correlates; the rarest word-frequency (Zipf) band a child reliably handles separates gifted lexical depth once common words ceiling. An adaptive staircase individualizes the frontier, making it less coachable than a fixed word list.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Run an adaptive frequency staircase over frequency-tagged word items (receptive vocab, opposites/synonyms, context cloze); record the lowest-frequency (rarest) band answered correctly at criterion.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=15-20 adaptive vocabulary items spanning several frequency bands to localize the ceiling with acceptable error.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Distractor lure profile
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Which class of distractor (phonological cousin, category/semantic cousin, thematic associate, surface match) pulls a child's errors reveals the grain of their semantic/relational discrimination; category-cousin near-misses at high difficulty indicate latent ability just below the cut, refining placement beyond right/wrong.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag every distractor with a lure class; on each error log the lure class chosen; aggregate the per-child error-by-lure distribution.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Every incorrect response; requires items built with a designed lure taxonomy; >=10-15 errors for a stable profile (pooled across verbal types).

tail_precision_rationale: Vocabulary ceiling is one of the cleanest verbal tail separators: once high-frequency words are trivial for a gifted child, only the rarest words discriminate. The frequency staircase drives each child to their personal lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH) instead of stopping at grade level, while lure-type analysis (M-LURETYPE) confirms that near-misses at ceiling are fine semantic discriminations (category cousin) rather than random taps, adding resolution exactly at the cut.
age_rationale: Point-to-picture receptive vocabulary needs no reading and only a single tap, so it works from K-1. It is retained through 4-5 with rarer words, but above 4-5 a pure picture-vocab task tends to ceiling and loses tail information for gifted readers, where meaning-in-context (Story Quest, Fill the Gap) carries more signal; hence 6-8 is excluded by design.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete high-frequency nouns/verbs (K-1) through low-frequency and abstract words depicted via small scenes (4-5); frequency-leveled by Zipf band.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency/rarity; abstractness (concrete object vs depicted action/attribute); semantic closeness of distractors; number of tiles (2->4->6); audio-only vs audio+scene.
adaptive.notes: Items auto-generated from a frequency-tagged word bank paired with an image library; parallel forms cloned by swapping same-frequency words and same-lure-class distractors.

engagement_hook: A safari photo hunt: each correct tap snaps a photo of the animal/thing into a sticker album, and rarer words earn shinier stickers, so climbing the vocabulary ladder is the reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Highest verbal risk is language background and print exposure (mitigated by audio prompts, frequency leveling, and dialect-neutral imagery); image ambiguity (mitigated by prototypical pictures per Rosch); motor mis-tap (large tiles, lock-to-confirm, revisions logged via M-REV); device audio quality (caption fallback + replay button).

name: Bridge Pairs
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_analogy
one_liner: See a top pair of pictures that go together, then pick the picture that makes the bottom pair go together the same way.
interaction: A 2x2 matrix: top-left -> top-right shows a relation (bird -> nest); bottom-left is given and bottom-right is blank with four picture choices below. The child taps a choice; an arrow animates the mapped relation and the tile locks. Young bands hear the relation frame; older bands use printed frequency-leveled word pairs.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the top pair connects with a glowing arrow, an identical arrow starts from the bottom-left, and the hand taps the picture that completes the same arrow. One unscored warm-up (dog->puppy, cat->?) with an obvious relation runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Analogy is aligning relational structure rather than surface features; young children reason relationally when the relation is familiar and depictable, letting us measure fluid verbal reasoning with almost no vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Relations use concrete, cross-culturally familiar pairs (animal->home, object->function) shown as pictures, so the near-language-free relation carries the item.
learning_science.source: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170.

learning_science.why: Children as young as 3-4 solve a:b::c:d analogies when the relations are within their knowledge, so picture analogies validly bridge pre-readers to older verbal analogies.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses picture relations; the identical shell swaps in printed frequency-leveled word pairs for 6-8, letting one type span all bands.
learning_science.source: Goswami, U. (1992). Analogical Reasoning in Children. Lawrence Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Zero written instructions and a single mapped arrow keep working memory on the relation instead of on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The animated arrow externalizes the relation frame; there is no instructional text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Because the relation, not vocabulary, carries the item, correct answers on multi-relation or abstract-relation analogies isolate fluid-verbal reasoning near the cut with minimal language confound. The distractor taxonomy (M-ERRTYPE: surface-match lure vs relational-reversal lure) reveals whether a near-miss reflects partial relational alignment (latent ability just under threshold) versus surface capture, and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separates reflective mappers from guessers at ceiling.
age_rationale: Picture analogies with familiar relations are solvable from K-1 (single tap, no reading). The same shell scales to 6-8 by increasing relational complexity and switching pictures to printed frequency-leveled word pairs; motor demand stays a single tap throughout.

adaptive.content_range: One concrete relation (animal->baby) up to abstract/double relations (tool->action->product) and printed word analogies across domains.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation abstractness; number of relations combined; surface similarity of distractors; picture vs printed-word stimuli; adding a second relational dimension.
adaptive.notes: AIG from a relation-typed pair bank; distractors auto-built as surface-match, relation-reversal, and associate lures.

engagement_hook: Build a glowing bridge between pictures: each correct pair snaps a plank into place and a character walks across; wrong planks wobble, right ones lock.
construct_irrelevant_risks: This is the near-language-free verbal option, so it is the anchor against language bias; residual risks are relation familiarity carrying culture (mitigated by universal relations and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST), surface-feature capture in young children (mitigated by the warm-up + arrow scaffold), reading load only in the 6-8 word mode (mitigated by frequency leveling + an audio option), and single-tap motor keeping motor noise low.

name: Club or Odd One
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_classification
one_liner: Find the picture or word that belongs with a group, or tap the one that does not fit.
interaction: Three stimuli that share a hidden property sit in a club; four candidates appear below. In Belongs mode the child taps the candidate that joins the club; in Odd-One mode four items show and the child taps the one to eject. The choice animates in/out and locks. Audio names the items for pre-readers; older bands use frequency-controlled words.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three fruits glow together, the hand taps the fourth fruit (it flies into the club) and pushes a shoe away. One unscored warm-up (three animals + one car) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Category membership is graded around prototypes, so measuring how a child groups items reveals concept formation independent of decoding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Groups are built around clear taxonomic categories for young bands and thematic/abstract categories for older, with member typicality controlled.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192-233.

learning_science.why: Choosing the odd item requires inducing the shared rule and testing candidates against it, which is core inductive reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log which candidates are sampled/hovered (M-EXPLORE) to distinguish systematic from random rule search.
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

learning_science.why: Removing written instructions keeps limited working memory on the category rule, not on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The club metaphor and animation teach the response with no instruction text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Distractors are built as competing-category lures (an item that fits a different but plausible rule). At the tail, choosing the target over a strong competing-category lure shows the child found the more specific/abstract shared rule; M-LURETYPE plus M-EXPLORE reveal whether high performers converge quickly on the correct rule while others sample widely, adding process resolution beyond accuracy at the cut.
age_rationale: Picture classification by taxonomic category is solvable at K-1; abstraction (function, thematic, superordinate) and printed-word items raise it to 6-8. A single tap throughout keeps motor demands flat.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete taxonomic categories -> abstract/superordinate and cross-domain word classes.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/abstract); member typicality; strength of the competing-category lure; picture vs word.
adaptive.notes: AIG from category-tagged banks; lures auto-selected from a sibling category to control near-miss meaning.

engagement_hook: A club-bouncer game: wave the right member in and bounce the impostor out; combos reward fast-correct choices without false ejections.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Category knowledge can reflect exposure/culture (mitigated by universal categories for young bands and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST); picture ambiguity (prototypical art); reading only in word mode at older bands (frequency-controlled list per the qbank); single-tap motor.

name: Spot the Silly
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_absurdities
one_liner: Find what is silly or impossible in a picture or short story, and for older kids show why.
interaction: A scene or short scenario is presented (audio + picture for young; text for older). The child taps the impossible element (a fish riding a bike) and it highlights. For 4-5 and 6-8 a second step asks why it is silly, answered by picture/choice (young) or a short typed reason (oldest), scored for the identified violation as partial credit.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a scene shows the sun wearing mittens; the hand taps the mittens and a giggle pop appears. One unscored warm-up (an upside-down umbrella catching rain) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Detecting an impossibility requires integrating each element against world knowledge; the speed and success of that integration index verbal reasoning and knowledge structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items embed a single well-defined world-knowledge violation and the response is tapping the violating element, separating detection from expressive language.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: Verbal Absurdities is a long-validated marker of verbal comprehension and reasoning in standardized batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep the classic construct but replace spoken-explanation scoring with taps plus an optional short justification to reduce expressive-language load for young and ELL children.
learning_science.source: Roid, G. H. (2003). Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5): Technical Manual. Riverside.

learning_science.why: Explaining why something is impossible requires building and checking a coherent mental model of the scenario, which is the deep-comprehension signal for the why step.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The why step is scored by inference depth (M-INFDEPTH), from naming the violation to explaining its consequence.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Inference depth level reached
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Comprehension discrimination at the tail is about inference layer, not literal recall; recording the deepest layer answered correctly (literal -> local/bridging inference -> global/thematic -> author's-purpose/evaluative) cleanly separates strong comprehenders who reach evaluative inference from those who plateau at literal.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag each comprehension/absurdity/cloze probe with an inference-depth level; record the maximum level answered correctly at criterion within a passage/unit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 probes spanning depth levels per passage/unit; several passages to stabilize the estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: The two-step design turns one item into a graded measure: detecting the anomaly (M-ACC) plus articulating the correct violation and its consequence (M-POLY, M-INFDEPTH). At the tail, gifted children not only spot subtle, plausibility-graded absurdities fast (M-RTFIRST) but explain the causal/logical reason, so inference-depth scoring separates saw it from understood why precisely where the cut sits.
age_rationale: Tap-the-silly picture works at K-1 (recognition only). The explanation step and text scenarios are added at 4-5 and deepened at 6-8; the pre-reader version needs no reading or expressive language.

adaptive.content_range: Obvious visual impossibilities -> subtle plausibility violations and multi-clause scenario absurdities.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: salience of the violation; number of plausible-but-fine elements (distractor density); picture -> audio -> text; required explanation depth.
adaptive.notes: Scene templates with a swappable violation slot; explanation rubric anchors define the partial-credit categories.

engagement_hook: A silly-detector meter that giggles and fills up when you catch the impossible thing; subtler absurdities are worth more giggles.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The why step adds expressive-language/writing load (mitigated by picture/choice justification for young bands, optional speech-to-text, and keeping typed reasons out of young bands); world knowledge can be cultural (mitigated by universal physical/biological violations); single-tap motor for detection.

name: Flip It
topics_techniques_covered: antonyms_synonyms
one_liner: Find the opposite, or the closest match, of a spoken or printed word.
interaction: A target is given (audio + picture for young; printed word for older). In Opposite mode the child taps the picture/word that means the reverse; in Match mode taps the closest-in-meaning option. The choice locks with a flip animation. A frequency staircase adjusts word rarity after each answer.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a big elephant target shows; the hand taps the tiny mouse and a flip animation plays (big <-> small). One unscored warm-up (up/down arrows) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Judging antonymy/synonymy is comparing shared versus contrasting semantic features, probing depth of lexical-semantic representation beyond merely knowing a word.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Opposites use a single contrasting dimension for young items (size, height) and multi-feature contrasts for older; synonyms control shared-feature distance.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.principle: Vocabulary as a reasoning/exposure proxy (Matthew effect)
learning_science.why: Depth and breadth of word-meaning relations predict verbal reasoning, but raw exposure must not be rewarded on its own.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Frequency-matched distractors and adaptive rarity ensure the score reflects semantic-relation reasoning (M-VOCABLVL) rather than simply having met the word.
learning_science.source: Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading. Reading Research Quarterly, 21(4), 360-407.

learning_science.why: Picture-opposite items let pre-readers show antonym reasoning without any print, verifying meaning across verbal and visual codes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio prompt + picture choices; printed words appear only from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Antonym/synonym items with frequency-matched lures push discrimination into fine semantic space; the adaptive rarity staircase locates the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL) while lure analysis (M-LURETYPE) flags whether ceiling errors are near-synonym confusions (fine-grained, latent ability) versus associative captures, sharpening placement right at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: Concrete picture opposites (big/small, up/down, happy/sad) are within K-1 grasp with audio; abstract antonyms and nuanced synonyms with printed words extend to 6-8. Single tap; reading load only in the older word mode.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete perceptual opposites -> abstract antonyms and nuanced synonyms.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency; abstractness; opposite vs synonym mode; semantic distance of the lure; picture vs word.
adaptive.notes: Antonym/synonym pair bank tagged by frequency and semantic distance; parallel clones swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: A mirror world where tapping the opposite flips the scene (day -> night); Match mode magnetizes twins together.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Opposition/synonymy is highly language- and culture-loaded (the highest-bias verbal skill; mitigated by audio and picture mode for young, frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral concepts); abstract relations are hard to depict (older bands use words); single-tap motor; guessing controlled via M-CONSIST parallel items.

name: Do What I Say
topics_techniques_covered: following_oral_directions
one_liner: Listen to a spoken instruction and tap the picture(s) that satisfy every condition.
interaction: A grid of pictures/shapes (varying size, color, position) is shown. Audio gives a multi-condition direction (tap the small blue star that is above the tree). The child taps the matching cell(s); multi-step directions require an ordered sequence of taps; a replay button repeats the audio once. Taps lock on submit.
